onesie is a command line tool that asks System One models typed questions about text. It needs the `onesie` binary on PATH and an API key, from TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Berget, Levanto or Cloudflare. This skill walks a user from nothing to a working first command.

typesafe is the default. For openrouter, store the key with `onesie --provider openrouter auth set`, and have the user add `export ONESIE_PROVIDER=openrouter` to their shell profile. Otherwise every command needs `--provider openrouter`, and without it onesie looks for a TypeSafe key and reports none. berget and levanto work the same way, with `onesie --provider berget auth set` and `export ONESIE_PROVIDER=berget`, or `onesie --provider levanto auth set` and `export ONESIE_PROVIDER=levanto`. For cloudflare, store the token with `onesie --provider cloudflare auth set --base-url https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/<account_id>/ai`, which keeps the account beside it, and have the user add `export ONESIE_PROVIDER=cloudflare` to their shell profile.

typesafe is the default and reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, plus `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` when they are set. openrouter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone, and never falls back to the TypeSafe key or those two variables. `jev-latest` works on both, but a pinned model id does not carry over: TypeSafe pins `jev-1.13.0`, OpenRouter pins `typesafe/jev-1.13`. berget reads `BERGET_API_KEY` alone and serves its own models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` names the rest. levanto reads `LEVANTO_API_KEY` alone and serves its Sage models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `sage-latest` alias. cloudflare reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, defaults to `typesafe/jev` through AI Gateway, which needs credits, and serves `clef`, `clef-flash` and `clef-omni`. It takes images but no Box or long context. `onesie auth status` names the provider and where its key came from.

The provider's variable: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for typesafe, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` for openrouter, `BERGET_API_KEY` for berget, `LEVANTO_API_KEY` for levanto, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` for cloudflare. No provider falls back to another's key.

A 401, a 403 or a 402. OpenRouter sends 402 when the account is out of credits, Berget when the key has no subscription, and Levanto when the period's included usage is used up, and Cloudflare when AI Gateway has no credits left for Jev.

The live suite asks the real APIs. It reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `LEVANTO_API_KEY`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` from the environment or from a gitignored `.env`, and skips the cases of a provider whose key is absent:

`TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `LEVANTO_API_KEY`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`: the weekly live suite in `.github/workflows/integration.yml`. The history lessons check uses `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.

Pipe in some text, ask a question, get an answer you can script against. Asks TypeSafe's Jev, directly or through OpenRouter or Cloudflare, Berget's own System One models, Levanto's Sage, or Cloudflare's Clef.

**Providers.** TypeSafe is the default, and `--provider openrouter`, `--provider berget`, `--provider levanto` or `--provider cloudflare` asks through OpenRouter, Berget, Levanto or Cloudflare instead. Cloudflare needs `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` beside its token.

Cloudflare takes images and no Box questions. Its Jev reads the `assets` map as TypeSafe does. Clef takes up to 4 images, which onesie sends in the order their names first appear, writing each name in the text as `image 1`, `image 2` and so on, so a question names an image as it does on TypeSafe.
`-i request` sends the images header only to TypeSafe, rewrites a body into inline parts for OpenRouter, and on Cloudflare sends Jev the assets as written and Clef numbered images.
onesie's image limits, which `onesie -V` lists, are TypeSafe's. They also apply on Cloudflare, where they are not measured for Clef.

Cloudflare also needs the account id, from `--base-url`, then `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, then a base URL stored with `onesie --provider cloudflare auth set --base-url https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/<account_id>/ai`. A stored base URL applies only to a stored key. `auth status` prints where the account comes from, and exits 2 when none does.

The Cloudflare token needs `Account` > `Workers AI` > `Read`. Its default model, `typesafe/jev`, is TypeSafe's Jev through AI Gateway, billed from AI Gateway credits, with a 32,000 token context and no choice of version. `clef`, `clef-flash` and `clef-omni` are Cloudflare's own models, run on the free daily Workers AI allowance, with contexts of 65,536, 24,576 and 65,536 tokens. `--list-models` lists them all.
Cloudflare takes no long context, so `--long-context` there exits 2 before any request.
A printed body is onesie's, not Cloudflare's envelope, so it replays through `-i request` with `--provider cloudflare`, not by curl.
TypeSafe says Unknown model, OpenRouter says the model does not exist, Berget answers 404 with Model not found, Levanto answers 422 with unknown model, and Workers AI answers 400 with No such model.
--base-url, the provider's base URL variable and its account variable stay ahead of the file's own base URL, so the stored one is only passed when none of them has anything to say.
Every body would be refused, so the run stops before it reads any.

A mock run resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts no requests, tokens or attempts, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions, 0s`.
The `--out` fingerprint marks the run as a mock, so a real run refuses to resume a mock run's file and the other way round. The mock file's content is not part of it.

`calibrate --mock` works, so a calibration can be tested too. Its `-o json` report carries `"mocked":true`. An entry may also answer the questions `calibrate` skips, so one mock file for a whole question file serves any set of labels. `--mock` and `ONESIE_MOCK` are refused beside `--print-request`, `-i request`, `--list-models` and every `auth` subcommand. The flag wins over the variable, and an empty `ONESIE_MOCK` is ignored.

One image under many names is one asset, which passes the body limit, and openrouter places it at every name, which does not.
Seeded, so the size is the same on every run. Noise does not compress, so the file stays near four bytes a pixel.
The checks a real run makes before it sends, so a mock refuses what the provider would.
A mock run and a real run never resume each other's file.

`--offline`, with `--out` and `--resume`, reads every answer from the file and asks nothing, so the check needs no key, costs nothing and never rewrites the file. A record the file does not answer, a missing file or a fingerprint that does not match exits 2. In CI that means the questions or the records changed, so rerun without `--offline` and commit the new file. The fingerprint names the model and the provider, so pin a versioned model such as `-m jev-1.13.0`, since an alias such as `jev-latest` moves on release. Have the user store the key in a profile, outside the conversation.
Run `onesie profile test` and confirm it reports the provider and a model count.
For a flag this skill does not cover, run `onesie --help`, `onesie profile --help` or `onesie calibrate --help`, and `onesie -V` for the version and the built in limits.

Anything typed into the conversation is sent to the model and kept in the transcript. `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER` reads the key from a hidden prompt in a real terminal, or from stdin otherwise, and never prints it. So ask the user to run it in their own terminal, or to pipe the key from a password manager, as in `pass show typesafe | head -n 1 | onesie profile create work --provider typesafe`. `pass show` and its siblings print metadata after the secret, and `profile create` refuses stdin that holds more than one non blank line, so keep the `head -n 1`. A profile names its provider, so `onesie profile create work --provider openrouter` makes an OpenRouter profile. The first profile becomes the default, and a run with no `--profile` uses the default. To switch to another profile, run `onesie profile use NAME`. Do not export `ONESIE_PROVIDER` for a stored key, since `--provider` and `ONESIE_PROVIDER` run without a profile and read only the provider's key variable. Berget lists its models to any key, so on berget it also asks one tiny question with the profile's model, which spends a few tokens. It exits 2 when no key resolves, 3 when the provider refuses the key or the keychain cannot give it up, and 4 or 5 when the provider cannot be reached. Only a clean `profile test` means the next real command will work.

A name in place of `work` is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, does not start with `-`, and is not `none`. A profile holds the provider, its key, and optionally `--model`, the model a run uses when it names none, and `--base-url`, or `--account-id` on cloudflare. `profile create` writes only to stderr, never the key:

A top level `assert` or `abstain_if` is the file's gate. An unknown key exits 2 rather than being ignored. Ahead of the message, which quotes the URL.
A flag given is a choice made, as an empty --profile is, so it is not read as unset.
A character device is not enough, since /dev/null is one and a hidden prompt cannot read it.
A character device that is not a terminal, as stdin is under < /dev/null.
An entry is named after its provider, so an unknown provider is an entry name, not a profile.
One profile at a time, so a misfit names the profile it is in.
A syntax error can quote a character of the file, which may be part of a key, so only an unknown member and a member of the wrong type, which name the member and not its value, are passed on.
ValidAccountID reports whether id is a Cloudflare account id, 32 hexadecimal characters.
WithRemove replaces how a Store deletes profiles.json, the credentials.json it replaces and a leftover temporary file.
Ahead of the mode check, since a directory or a device node is not a config file at a bad mode, and no chmod 600 would fix it.
0o077 rather than 0o044. A group writable profiles.json or credentials.json is as bad as a readable one, since whoever can replace it can substitute a key whose traffic they see.
ReadableError means a file's mode lets someone other than its owner reach it. Kind names the file, as profiles file or credential file.

A yes or no question answers with how likely the yes is. `-r` prints only the answer. Without it, the table for a pick or a rate also shows the model's confidence and the probability of each option or level.

Every output format writes each number of an answer as `-o json` does, in the shortest form that reads back as that number. A number the provider sent prints as sent, never rounded, so how many places it carries is the provider's and the model's: TypeSafe's Jev sends two where another model may send more. A number onesie computes itself, such as `norm` or a mock's `p` and `score`, is rounded to four places when it is computed. So the table, markdown, csv and json show `0.7` alike, and a printed number is the one a gate compares.

`--assert` is one boolean over the record, and it sets the exit code. It reads the field names `-o json` prints, and every path is checked before any request. So is every string compared with a pick or rate `value` by `==`, `!=` or `in`, which must name one of its options or levels:

A question id may hold any character, but a path reaches it by its bare name only when it is letters, digits and `_`, starts with a letter or `_`, and is not one of `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`, `true` and `false`. Write any other id in brackets and double quotes, as in `["needs review"].value` or `["a-b"].value`, and an option or level the same way after `p`, as in `team.p["on call"]`. An id written bare that only the bracket form reaches exits 2 and shows the bracket form.

A yes or no answer is a probability, or an object whose `value` is one. A pick or rate answer is a name, or an object with `value` and an optional `confidence`, which defaults to 1. With no `p`, the value's probability is the confidence, or twice what each other option or level gets when that is more, rounded up to four places, so it is never below the confidence. The others share the rest evenly in steps of 0.0001, the first of them taking one step more where it does not divide evenly. So the value is always the most likely, and the `p` printed replays. A rate's `score` is the level index averaged over `p`, rounded to four places, unless the entry gives one. A number whose text is a name is that name, so `4` rates `--rate 1,2,3,4,5`. A rate question from a request body takes its level index.

The other keys `-o json` writes are accepted. A line's `model`, `usage`, `line`, `assert` and `abstain` are ignored, since the gate runs again. Inside an answer, `decision`, `fallback` and `legend` are ignored. A rate's `score` and `norm` are replayed, a `norm` written exactly or rounded to four places alike, and so is a pick or rate's `p`, whose keys must be exactly the options or levels, whose values lie between 0 and 1, and whose most likely entry is the value. So a replay prints what the real run printed, and a gate that reads `p` decides the same way.

A mock run chooses its profile and resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a `--profile` that does not exist, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads `profiles.json` unless `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses the run. A test can point `ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR` at a fixture of its own, at mode `600`, whose profile holds a dummy `api_key`, since every profile must hold a key. A mock run uses no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts no requests, tokens or attempts, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions answered, 0s`.

stdin is never read beside `--image`, so text joins it only from `--state`, `--state-file` or `--state -`. Text goes under the key `text`, a JSON object gains the image keys, and a key clash or an array state exits 2. An `-i` given beside `--image` with neither `--state` nor `--state-file` exits 2, since there is no stdin for it to read, and names `--state -`.

`--cache`, or `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, stores each successful response on disk and answers a repeated request from it. Without either, nothing is stored and nothing is read. `ONESIE_CACHE` takes the values the flag takes, such as `1`, `true`, `0` and `false`, and anything else exits 2 in every run and `calibrate`, `--mock` and `--print-request` included. `--cache=false` turns the cache off for one run under `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, so that run asks the API again.

On the `typesafe` provider, a model name that ends in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned, and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on any other provider, `typesafe/jev-1.13` on OpenRouter and `Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B` on Berget and `levanto-sage-v1.4` on Levanto included. An alias's answers expire after 24 hours, since the model behind it can move. `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` sets that lifetime as a duration, such as `90m` or `72h`, and `0` stops reading and storing answers for an alias. A negative or malformed value exits 2, in every run whether or not it uses the cache, in `onesie cache` and in `onesie cache clear`. A run's lifetime decides what it reads, not what it deletes: an expired answer is only a miss, which the next answer overwrites, and onesie deletes an alias's answer only once it is older than 24 hours, or than the run's own lifetime when that is longer. So a short lifetime in one run never deletes answers other runs still read. An answer stored at a time later than the clock reads is a miss too.

Its files are mode `600` in directories of mode `700`. `--cache` refuses a cache directory others can reach with exit 2, before any request. Windows carries no such modes, so the check is skipped there. onesie writes a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, so backup tools skip the cache, into a new cache directory and into an existing one that is empty or holds only what onesie writes. `--cache` refuses an existing directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` that holds anything else with exit 2, before any request, since a tag there would hide those files from backup tools, and entries stored without one could never be cleared. onesie counts, evicts and clears only its own entries and temporary files, and leaves anything else in a tagged directory alone. Writes are atomic, so parallel runs can share one cache.

`jev-latest` works on typesafe and openrouter, but pinned ids differ: `jev-1.13.0` on TypeSafe, `typesafe/jev-1.13` on OpenRouter. Berget serves its own models and not `jev-latest`. Its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` there lists only the System One models, each with its aliases. Levanto also serves its own models and not `jev-latest`. Its default is the `sage-latest` alias, and an unknown model there is a 422 rather than a 400. On OpenRouter, `--usage` also reports the cost, which the `-o table` header and `--stats` show too. A 200 whose answers onesie cannot use still spent its tokens, so under `--usage` its json error record carries them too, and `--stats` counts them. `-o values`, `-o raw`, `-r`, `-o csv` and `-o tsv` have no place for `--usage`, and `-q` writes nothing, so they all refuse it with exit 2.

`--stats` writes a one line summary to stderr, as in `6 records, 2 skipped by --resume, 1 cached, 3 requests, 3 questions asked, 412 in / 9 out tokens, model jev-latest, 4 attempts (1 retry: 429×1), 10s/attempt, 2.1s`. The records lead with every one the run read, and the counts after them are parts of that whole: those `--resume` skipped, the cache answered, deduplication shared, that failed, and the requests sent. A run of one record that became one request leads with `1 request` alone. The questions are those the requests asked, so a cache hit asks none. The tokens and the cost OpenRouter reports are summed over the requests, and the per attempt timeout is left out of a run that made no attempt.

An error response whose body is not JSON, such as the HTML page a web server sends for a wrong path, prints its status and says the body is not JSON, as in `onesie: 405 Method Not Allowed, with a response body that is not JSON. Check that the base URL points at the System One API`. A page is left out, and only the first line of a plain text body is kept. Only a 404 or a 405 adds the hint to check the base URL, since an outage, a rate limit or a refused key comes from the right server too. A body sent as JSON that holds only a string prints the first line of that string after the status.

`onesie --help` lists every flag, and `onesie -V` prints the built in limits. `-V` takes no question, so a word beside it exits 2. `onesie help calibrate` prints a subcommand's help, and a topic that names no subcommand exits 2.
Rounded rounds a number onesie computes itself to four places, so a gate, -o json and the table all see the same value rather than float noise.
Number writes a number of an answer as -o json does, in the shortest form that reads back as the same number and never rounded, so every output mode shows the number a gate compares.
Switch returns a pflag value like Flag's for a flag that takes no value, so the help shows none.
pflag prints a bool flag whose NoOptDefVal is true with no value at all.
BracketHint advises the bracket form for the first id in ids that source writes bare, although only the bracket form can reach it. It returns the empty string when there is none.
model stands for a string, since a string literal must also name an option when it meets a pick or rate value.
Open opens the cache in dir, creating it with mode 700 and a CACHEDIR.TAG when it is missing. It refuses a directory others can reach, except on windows, and an untagged one holding foreign files.

A directory holding nothing but what onesie writes gets its tag, so clear can empty it later. One holding anything else may not be onesie's. A tag there would hide the foreign files from backup tools, and storing without one would leave entries clear refuses to remove.
ForeignError means the cache directory holds files onesie did not write and no CACHEDIR.TAG, so it may not be onesie's to fill.
Error names the directory and the fix.
onesie-go decodes a JSON string body and a body that is not JSON alike, so only the content type tells a server's quoted message from a page a proxy sent.
An HTML page from a proxy or a web server says nothing a terminal line can show, while a one line text body may name the cause.
Only a missing path or method points at the base URL. An outage, a rate limit or a refused key arrives from the right server too.

A cache others can read, a directory that may not be onesie's, or a lifetime onesie cannot read is something the user asked for and has to fix, so each ends the run. Any other failure only turns the cache off.
-V answers before any question is read, so its own message names what it refuses.
Not cobra's own version flag, which prints before any argument is checked.
Cobra would add completion only when the tree runs, after the walk below.
pflag keeps no spelling for a value it refused, so the command line says which one was typed. A long form is matched first, since a value such as -just can look like a cluster of shorthands.

cobra.NoArgs speaks in cobra's terms, as in unknown command "x" for "onesie version". Any other validator's message is kept as written, since the sentences below fit only a command that takes no argument.
A caller that names the path already, as in reading X, makes the copy the PathError carries, as in open X, say the same thing twice.
Records is every input record a resume did not skip. Requests is the subset that reached the client, which is smaller whenever a line failed to parse, the cache answered or a request was shared.
Questions counts the questions the requests asked, so a record the cache answered adds none.
Cost is the summed cost the provider reported, which only OpenRouter does, and nil otherwise.

A non streaming run has one record and one request and says so once. A stream reports both only when they differ, which is exactly when a record never became a request. The records lead with every one the run read, those a resume skipped included, so each count after them reads as a part of that whole.
A run that made no attempt waited on none, so a per attempt timeout would describe nothing.
a scores 0.7*0.9 + 0.3*(1 - 0.3333) = 0.83001, with norm rounded to four places, and b scores 0.7*0.4 + 0.3*1 = 0.58.
onesie rounds the norm it prints to four places, and an older one printed it exact, so either replays.
A written p need not add up to 1, so the average is taken over what it holds.

At least twice what each other name takes keeps the value the strict mode, which replayed demands of a written p, since a rate reads its value from the first of equal modes. Counted in units of 0.0001, the value keeps its share exactly and the others split the rest, the first of them taking one unit more where it does not divide evenly.
Rounded up, so a confidence with more than four places never rises above the value's p. The small allowance keeps float noise, as in 0.6 times 10000, from rounding up a whole unit.
Cost writes a cost in dollars, rounded to the hundred millionth, which keeps a provider's float noise out of a line meant for people.
Two leading spaces, the space after the label and the space before the number.
A norm replays whether it is exact or rounded to four places, the form onesie prints.

`--print-request` over a stream writes one body per input line, and `-i request` reads those bodies back. It checks that each line is one JSON object and still applies the flag rules, but nothing inside the body: no question checks, no normalization and no policy. So a bad body is sent as is and comes back as an error record, not an exit 2, and a good one comes back as the raw response body, not the usual record. A response that is not a System One result, or whose answers do not fit the body's questions, is an error line of kind response instead. The one change is a body whose `model` is missing, empty, all whitespace or null, which takes the run's resolved model. Under `-i request`, `--print-request` prints each body as it would be sent, so adding it to a pipeline turns the whole run into a dry run: `onesie --ask urgent='is this urgent' -i jsonl --print-request < in.jsonl > bodies.jsonl && onesie -i request < bodies.jsonl`.

For one record, onesie reads stdin beside --image only through --state -, so text joins the image only from --state, --state-file or --state -. A stream, -i jsonl, lines, csv or tsv, still reads its records from stdin and adds the image to each. TypeSafe calls images and Box dreamer ready, an experimental stage, so expect them to be less reliable than text. A Box always returns a box, even when the target is not in the image, so ask a yes or no question about whether it is there in the same call and read the box only when it says yes. -r prints a box as left, top, right and bottom, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner. TypeSafe and OpenRouter read images and Box. Levanto and Berget refuse both before any request.

**Wire the gate into a script.** Exit 0 runs the command, 1 blocks it and 7 asks a person. Any other exit code means there was no answer. Exit 4 includes a 200 whose answer did not fit the question, which onesie never retries.

An empty or all whitespace question exits 2 before any request, the way an empty state does, whether it came from the positional argument, `--ask`, a question file's `ask` or the `instructions` of a `-f` request body. So does a null or missing question, one that is a number or `true` or `false`, and an empty mapping or sequence. A `-f` body question that carries `ask` in place of `instructions` exits 2 and says so. An `-i request` body is forwarded as it is and not checked, apart from a `model` that is missing, empty, all whitespace or null, which onesie fills in.

A pick or rate answer carries `confidence`, a number from 0 to 1 the API computes from `p`. In the committed rate answers it is about 1 when `p` sits on one level, never above the top probability, and lower as the rest spreads to other levels, most of all to far ones. `--min-confidence` cuts on it. A yes or no answer carries no confidence. The API always sends `confidence`, and onesie reads one it leaves out as 0, the least confident value, since the decoder cannot tell it from a sent 0. So `--min-confidence` falls back on it and a gate on `confidence` does not pass. A mock entry's default of 1 is only shorthand for writing the mock.

Every answer is checked against the question asked before it is printed, gated or cached, on a plain run, in a stream, under `-q` and `--assert`, in `calibrate` and when the cache is read. A yes or no value, each `p` and each `confidence` lies in [0,1], a pick names one of its options, a rate's `score` lies between 0 and its top level index, the keys of `p` are exactly the options, or the level indexes from 0 for a rate, and `p` adds up to 1 within half a hundredth per entry, and at least a hundredth. An answer of the wrong type fails too. Any of these exits 4 with `200 response could not be used:` and names the question and the value, as in `question 'urgent' answered 1.5, which lies outside [0,1]`. In a stream the record is an error line of kind `response`. Its tokens still count toward `--usage` and `--stats`, it is never stored in the cache, and it is not retried, since the same request would get the same answer.

`--box` makes a question a box, answered with `left`, `top`, `right` and `bottom`, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner, and a `confidence`. It needs an image, as in Images below, and a provider that takes it, TypeSafe or OpenRouter, as on `typesafe/jev-1.14`. Cloudflare, Levanto and Berget refuse it before any request. On TypeSafe the model must serve it too: one that does not answers 400 `Invalid request`, and onesie then names `-m jev-preview`, which does. It takes no value and no `--desc`, `--threshold`, `--min-confidence` or `--fallback`. `-r` prints the four edges in that order, and `-o csv` writes them as four columns, `ID_left`, `ID_top`, `ID_right` and `ID_bottom`. A box always returns a box, even when the target is not there, so pair it with a yes or no question that asks whether it is.

The other keys `-o json` writes are accepted. A line's `model`, `usage`, `line`, `assert` and `abstain` are ignored, since the gate runs again. Inside an answer, `decision`, `fallback` and `legend` are ignored. A rate's `score` and `norm` are replayed, a `norm` written exactly or rounded to four places alike, and so is a pick or rate's `p`, whose keys must be exactly the options or levels, whose values lie between 0 and 1 and add up to 1 within the rounding a live answer may carry, and whose most likely entry is the value. So a replay prints the answers the real run printed, and a gate that reads `p` decides the same way. The `model` it prints is the one the mock run resolved, not the one the record holds, so an alias such as `jev-latest` stays an alias.

Each requirement that did not hold is named on stderr with the four place numbers it compared, its value, interval and cut, as in `'u.catches >= 0.9' did not hold: 3/4 is 0.75, interval 0.3006 to 0.9544, at cut 0.50`, or `AUC 0.9993` for `auc`. A failed record still exits 6, which wins over 1.

The `-o json` report gains a `require` array, one entry per requirement: `{"expr":"u.catches >= 0.9 at 0.5","held":false,"value":0.6667,"interval":[0.2077,0.9385],"cut":0.5}`, for 2 of 3 caught. Each rate, interval end, `auc` and mean distance is rounded to four places when it is computed, so a requirement compares the number the `-o json` report prints. A rate, interval end or `auc` that is not exactly 0 or 1 never rounds to 0 or 1, so 29999 of 30000 is `0.9999`. The table report shows each rate and interval end as a whole percent, and adds one or two places to a share when whole percents would show a share that is not exactly 0 or 1 as 0 or 100, or two different numbers as the same, so `1/1000` reads `0.10% 0.02-0.56%`. It shows `auc` to 2 places, so it can read a little apart from the number compared. `auc` has `"interval":null`, a pick or rate measure `"cut":null`, and a measure over no records `"value":null` with a `reason`.

For one record, stdin is read beside `--image` only through `--state -`, so text joins the image only from `--state`, `--state-file` or `--state -`. Text goes under the key `text`, a JSON object gains the image keys, and a key clash or an array state exits 2. `-i text` or `-i json` beside `--image` with neither `--state` nor `--state-file` exits 2 and names `--state -`.
A stream, `-i jsonl`, `-i lines`, `-i csv` or `-i tsv`, reads its records from stdin as usual beside `--image`, and adds the same image to every record.

`--image-field NAME` reads each record's `NAME` as a path, in a stream or in `calibrate`. Under `-i lines` the line is the path, and only one `--image-field` is taken. A missing or unreadable file is an input error line, and the run goes on and exits 6.

Under `-i request` onesie does not check the body it sends, apart from filling a blank `model`, but it checks each 200 that comes back before printing it. A response that is not JSON, that is not a System One result with an `answers` object, or whose answers do not decode, is an error line of kind `response` with `200 response could not be used:`, and the run exits 6. When the body's `questions` read as a `-f` body's would, each answer is also checked against its question as on any other run, so a missing answer or a value out of its range fails the same way. A body whose questions onesie cannot read, such as one past `max-question-file-bytes`, gets only the first checks. The tokens of a refused response still count toward `--stats`.
`update` with a member set to the value it already has, or cleared when it is already unset, leaves the file alone, says so on stderr and exits 0. `update` with no member at all exits 2.

`show` never reads the keychain or prints a key. `key:` is `keychain` or `file`, with `, ends in XXXX` when the key has 16 characters or more, `env` and the key variable for a run without a profile, or `none`. A converted keychain key shows no ending until `onesie profile update NAME --key`. `chosen by:` is `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE`, `the default`, `--provider`, `ONESIE_PROVIDER` or `nothing`, and `not active` for a named profile a run would not use. `model:` and `base_url:` give the value a run would use, in the order a run picks it, then where it comes from: `profile`, `env TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL`, `env TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, `account_id`, `env CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `the provider's default`, as in `model: jev-latest, the provider's default`. `base_url:` is `none` on cloudflare with no account. An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters.

An empty or whitespace only variable counts as unset. An empty or whitespace only flag value exits 2 instead, since a flag given is a choice made. That holds for `--profile`, `--provider`, `--base-url`, `-m`, `--mock`, `-f`, `-i`, `-o`, `--out`, `--state-file`, `--map`, `--id`, `--merge-key`, `--image-field` and calibrate's `--label`, so `--mock "$UNSET"` never reaches the API. An empty `--sep` exits 2 too. `profile update` is the exception, where an empty value clears a member.

A question file carries no model, since `model` is a reserved question id there. Only a request body, as `--print-request` writes it, names one. Under `-i request` each body sends the model it names, and a body that names none, or an empty, all whitespace or null one, takes the profile's `model`, then the order above. Only the key `model` spelled in that case counts, so a body that holds only `Model` names none, and every blank `model` key in a body is filled. onesie writes that model into the body, so `--print-request` shows it too.

A run that `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses, and that succeeds, never opens `profiles.json`, so CI that names its provider does not depend on any file on the machine. Only a run that then fails for a missing key or an unknown provider reads it, to name a profile in the hint. Under `ONESIE_PROVIDER` with no profile for that provider, the hint names the key variable and says a stored profile is not used while the variable is set.

`-f VALUE` reads VALUE as a file when one exists at that path. Otherwise a bare name loads `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json` from the nearest `.onesie/questions`, then from `questions` in the config dir, and last takes a starter set built into onesie: `moderation`, `personal-data`, `prompt-injection` or `shell-safety`. A saved file wins over a built-in set of the same name, so a copy to edit is printed elsewhere first, as in `onesie -f shell-safety --print-questions > shell-safety.yaml`, then moved with `mv shell-safety.yaml .onesie/questions/`. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions` empties the file before onesie runs, and `-f` then finds that empty file ahead of the built-in set. `onesie questions` lists every name `-f` finds, with a built-in set shown as `built in` and an empty saved file marked `empty`, or `"empty":true` under `-o json`. A question file is refused with exit 2 when it is empty, when it uses a YAML alias or when it is larger than `max-question-file-bytes`, and every error in a file names its path. A file that holds no question, such as `{}` or only comments, adds nothing beside `--ask`, and on its own it exits 2, naming the file. An empty one is named, with how to reach the built-in set it hides.

`-f` also takes a request body, as `--print-request` writes it, a positional question's body keyed `answer` included. For one record, a body that holds a `state` sends that state, and onesie then never reads stdin, since it cannot tell a pipe that holds text from one that is still open without waiting on it. `--state` or `--state-file` beside such a body exits 2, naming both. `-i request` refuses both flags the same way, since each body there holds its own state. A stream and `calibrate` read their records from stdin as usual and send each one as its state, so they use the body only for its questions, and say on stderr that its state is ignored. A body's `assets` are sent with it. When its state is ignored, an asset only that state named is dropped, and the warning counts it.

`--long-context`, or `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, raises the context limits to 262k tokens, which is slower and less accurate. It is written into a printed body as `long_context`, so a replay keeps it, and a `-f` body's `long_context: true` turns it on with no flag. A body's `false` does not turn off the flag or the variable. The flag wins over the variable, so `--long-context=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, as `--cache=false` does for the cache. It does not turn off a body's `long_context: true`, from `-f` or under `-i request`, since the body asks for it itself. Set that key to `false` in the body, or remove it, to run without it. `-i request` follows the same order for each body it replays, and under `--print-request` it writes `"long_context":true` into a body the flag or the variable turns it on for. A provider that takes no long context refuses the run with exit 2, and when `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT` turned it on, the message says so. It is experimental on TypeSafe's side.

`onesie --help` lists every flag, and `onesie -V` prints the built in limits. A flag onesie does not know exits 2, naming the closest one when one is near. A flag that belongs to a run, given to a subcommand, says so, and on a bare subcommand name such as `onesie cache --model x` it also says how to ask that word as a question. `-V` takes no question, so a word beside it exits 2. `onesie help calibrate` prints a subcommand's help, and a topic that names no subcommand exits 2.

To edit a set, save a copy into `.onesie/questions/`. A saved file wins over the built-in set of the same name, so print the copy elsewhere and move it in. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions/` would empty the file before `-f` read it:

An answer that does not fit the question is deterministic, so it is a 200 whose body onesie could not use rather than a transport failure. That gives it kind response in a stream and exit 4 in a single shot run, and the same retry would only get it again.
checkChoice proved the keys are exactly the options, so the plan's order is the whole set.
SumFits reports a distribution's sum, rounded to four places, and whether it is 1 within the rounding a provider that writes two places per entry can leave, half a hundredth each, at least 0.01.
The last option takes the rest, so the distribution adds up to 1 as Normalize requires.
Comparisons take no tolerance, so that the ordered and the equality readings of one pair of numbers can never disagree, which is what this holds them to.
Every key but the winner carries no mass.
The four place numbers the requirement compared, not the table's percents, so a miss by less than a percent still shows.
AUC is the chance a random yes case outranks a random no case, a tie counting half, rounded as a share is. It is undefined unless both labels occur.
One no tied with the lowest yes, which counts half a pair of 22500.

Whole percents unless they would hide something: a share that is not none reading 0, one that is not all reading 100, or two different numbers reading the same. A four place share is exact at two places, so the search always ends.
From the four place value in whole hundredths of a percent, since 0.565 times 100 lands just under 56.5 in floating point and would round down.
Wilson returns hits of of as a share with its 95 percent Wilson score interval, each rounded to four places and never to 0 or 1 unless it is exactly that. A share of nothing is not Defined.
A share that is not all or none must not print as one, or 29999 of 30000 would read as every record and pass a requirement of 1.
A body of only Unauthorized, or of 401 Unauthorized, adds nothing to the status already named.
Not a request to check the key, which the server's own message often already makes.
onesie-go reports a body that did not decode with the decoder's own sentence, which names Go types. The fields it names are the wire's, so they are said again in the response's terms.
onesie-go names the answer as answer "x": ahead of the decoder's sentence.
An entry stored before a check onesie now makes would fail every run until it expires, so one that fails is passed over and replaced by a fresh answer.
Stored before the answer checks, so it reads back now as one they refuse.
The picked key takes p and the rest share what is left, so the distribution adds up to 1.

onesie-go calls every refused base URL not absolute and echoes it with a trailing slash trimmed, which reads wrong for one that has a scheme but no host, or that does not parse. The URL as the user gave it is echoed instead, since credentials were refused before this point.
The variable is easy to forget once it is exported, so a refusal it caused says so.
The same order onesie-go refuses in, since a Box question is an image question too. The message names only what the run needs, and the providers that take all of it.
The loader names the file ahead of its own sentence, and the rules match that sentence.
A name that starts with a dash reaches pflag first, which reads it as flags. The mark lets the flag error give the name rule instead.
A member named with the value it already has is a choice the file already holds, so it is noted rather than refused. Naming none is still a mistake.
A missing account prints as none and exits 2 below. One that is there but malformed fails a run the same way, so show names it rather than print a base_url of none.
A file of only comments reads as null, which holds no more than an empty mapping does.
An empty file beside --ask only adds nothing, which is fine. Alone it is the whole run, so the file is what to name.
A file that cannot be read is listed as it is, since -f reports why when it reaches it.
Resolved for --print-request too, which prints the model a body that names none is sent with.
--print-request prints the body as it would be sent, with exit 0 and no network. The same predicate decides this and the client above, so the two cannot disagree and leave a nil client.
The client refuses what the route cannot take in its own words, which name too few of the providers that can.

The body is otherwise sent as written, so the model goes in place or in front rather than through a decode and encode that would reorder the keys and reformat the numbers. Every empty model key is filled, since a server may read the first or the last of them.
A printed body carries long context as -f prints it, so a replay keeps what this run sends, and a body's own false does not turn off the flag or the variable.

A scan of a body json.Valid passed, rather than a decode, so the assets a body carries are walked past and never copied. Only the exact key counts, since encoding/json would match Model for model too and the API reads only the exact one.
A model name is short, so a long value is no blank one and is not decoded.
Only a body whose questions onesie can read, as -f reads one, says what each answer must fit.
An empty config dir, so the developer's own profiles never choose the model a body takes.
A flag given is a choice made, as an empty --profile is, so it is not read as unset. An unset variable in a script would otherwise drop a --mock and send a paid request.
A word that holds a space is a question the dash question hint speaks to.
With no word, it reports whether the command line holds any positional at all. A flag the subcommand does not know may still be the root's, which takes the next word as its value.
A word typed after two dashes was meant as a flag, so the allowance is wider than the one a bare word gets against the subcommands.
pflag names only the shorthands left when it stopped, so the command line says which word they ended, as -qz does for z.
Only a bare subcommand name could have been meant as a one word question. A deeper subcommand, or one given a word of its own, was meant as that subcommand.
Each body names its own model or takes the run's, and the fingerprint holds no model, as it holds nothing else a body carries.
A profile created now would still go unused while the variable chooses the run.

A run of one record that became one request says so once. Any other run leads with the records, every one it read, those a resume skipped included, so each count after them reads as a part of that whole. A mock run says how many the mock answered in the same clause when that is all of them.
A written p adds up to 1 only within the rounding SumFits allows, so the average is taken over what it holds.
The same rule the answer check applies at run time, so a mock it would refuse exits 2 here.

The positional question is keyed answer by design, so the reserved list only applies to an id the user chose. A request body may carry answer, since --print-request writes a positional question under it and -f reads that body back.

For a yes or no question the report has one row per cut. A row flags a record when `value >= cut`, the same test `--threshold 0.8` and `--assert 'urgent.value >= 0.8'` apply, so the cut goes into the gate as written. `catches` is the share of labelled yes records flagged, `false alarms` the share of labelled no records flagged, and `right when flagged` the share of flagged records labelled yes. Each shows the count, the share and its 95 percent interval, and on a few records the interval is the part to read: `2/2 99% 34-99%` says little. `worst misses` lists by id the records answered furthest from their label, each with the start of its mapped text on one line. Read them: a wrong label is fixed in the data, and a real miss means the question needs rewording and another calibration. A pick or rate question reports its agreement, a row per name with `found`, the share of the records labelled with it that were picked as it, and `right when picked`, the share of the records picked as it that carry its label, a table of labelled against picked, and one row per confidence cut with the share it answers and their agreement, which is where a `--min-confidence` comes from. The cuts run from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, and `--cuts 0.5,0.7,0.9` names your own.

`--require` turns the report into a check. The report still prints, each requirement that did not hold is named on stderr, and the run exits 1. A requirement reads `[lower|upper](ID.MEASURE) OP NUMBER [at CUT]`. The measures are `catches`, `false_alarms`, `right_when_flagged` and `auc` for a yes or no question, `agreement` for pick and rate, and `within_one` for rate. NUMBER is a fraction, so `95` exits 2. On a few records the plain value passes on luck, since 16 of 16 is a value of 1. `lower()` compares the low end of the 95 percent interval instead, 81 percent for 16 of 16, so `lower(urgent.catches) >= 0.9` fails until there are enough labelled records to back it. `lower` takes `>=` or `>`, `upper` takes `<=` or `<`, as in `upper(urgent.false_alarms) <= 0.1 at 0.9`, and `auc` has no interval. Without `at`, the cut comes from the `-f` file's `assert` when it compares `ID.value < X` or `ID.value >= X`, and `at abstain` takes it from the file's `abstain_if`. A missing cut exits 2 before any request.

`profile show` only reports what a run would use and where its key lives, and never reads the keychain. `profile test` reads the key and sends it to the provider's model listing, which costs no tokens, then prints `profile:`, `provider:`, `key:` and `models:` with a count. On berget it also asks one tiny question with the profile's model, which spends a few tokens. It exits 2 when no key resolves, 3 when the provider refuses the key or the keychain cannot give it up, and 4 or 5 when the provider cannot be reached. Only a clean `profile test` means the next real command will work.

`--out FILE` writes the answers to a file instead of stdout, with a fingerprint in `FILE.onesie` beside it. The fingerprint covers the questions, the provider, the model, `--map`, `--id`, the input and output modes, the merge key, the policy flags, `--assert` and `--abstain-if`, and `--skip-blank` when a resume counts lines, which is without `--id` on any input but csv and tsv. So `-j`, `--timeout` and `--retries` can change between runs, and `--skip-blank` can change with `--id` or on csv or tsv input. `--resume` exits 2 when any of those changed, saying `the questions, flags or gate changed`, or when a non empty file has no fingerprint or one from another onesie version, and says to drop `--resume` to start over. With `--id` a resume skips every record whose id the file already answers, with no request, and asks the rest, including a record whose last line was an error. Each answer is appended as it arrives, so an interrupted run loses nothing. Only a run with both `--resume` and `--id` rewrites the file once it completes, in input order with the newest line per id, and keeps the answered ids the input no longer holds after the rest, so a cut short input never deletes an answer. `--prune` drops those instead. `--resume` on a missing or empty file starts fresh, so pass it on the first run too. Until the rewrite the file can hold a record twice and out of order. Only the id is compared, so a record whose content changed but whose id stayed the same keeps its old answer. A skipped record keeps its stored assertion outcome, so it still counts toward exit 1 or 7 and toward `--stats`, and under `--stop-on-assert` a skipped false assertion stops the run with nothing after it asked. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume without `--id` drops a trailing error line and asks its record again, since a run stopped by `--stop-on-error` writes nothing after it, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it came from a run without `--stop-on-error`, and the resume stops there before any request, with the code that run exited with, or with exit 2 for a csv or tsv row, which keeps only the failure's message. Pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. With `--id` the failed record is asked again and stops the run only if it fails again. `--unordered` is allowed since the rewrite restores the order. Raw output is refused in every resume, with `--resume needs output that keeps each record's outcome, which raw lines do not`, since a raw line keeps no id, failure or gate outcome. A second run into the same `--out` file exits 2 until the first ends. A device or a pipe, such as `/dev/stdout`, gets no fingerprint and no lock, and `--resume` refuses one. A file or a directory onesie cannot write exits 2 before any request. Without `--id`, `--resume` counts the complete lines instead, drops a line cut off mid write, skips that many input records, retries no failed one but a trailing error line under `--stop-on-error`, and refuses `--unordered`. A stored error line it skips still counts as a failed record, so the run exits 6 and `--stats` counts it as failed, under `-i request` too. A full resume by id: `onesie 'is this urgent' -i jsonl -j 8 --map '.body' --id '.id' --out answers.jsonl --resume < tickets.jsonl`.

A bare question returns `value`, a probability from 0 to 1, and no confidence. `--pick` returns `value`, the winning name, with `confidence` and `p`, the probability of each option. `confidence` comes from the API, and is lower as `p` spreads across the options or levels. `--rate` returns `value`, the most likely level, with `score`, the level index averaged over `p` with 0 for the lowest level, so it can land between levels, `norm`, the score over the top index, from 0 to 1, `confidence` and `p`. A policy flag adds `decision` and `fallback`, covered in the onesie-gate skill, and `-o values` then prints the decision in place of the value. Each option and level loses the spaces around it, so `--pick 'yes, no'` names `yes` and `no`, and an empty name exits 2. When a name holds a comma, set another separator first, as in `--sep '|' --pick 'yes, refund|no, keep'`.

For one record, onesie reads stdin beside --image only through --state -, so text joins the image only from --state, --state-file or --state -. A stream, -i jsonl, lines, csv or tsv, still reads its records from stdin and adds the image to each. Images and Box are experimental on TypeSafe's side, so expect them to be less reliable than text. A Box always returns a box, even when the target is not in the image, so ask a yes or no question about whether it is there in the same call and read the box only when it says yes. -r prints a box as left, top, right and bottom, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner. TypeSafe and OpenRouter read images and Box. Levanto and Berget refuse both before any request.

`--print-questions > q.yaml` writes the questions, their descriptions, their policy flags and any assertion as YAML, and `onesie -f q.yaml` reads it back. The first line, `# yaml-language-server: $schema=URL`, lets an editor check the file against the JSON Schema that `onesie --print-schema` prints. Each top level key is a question id holding `ask` and optionally `pick` or `rate`, `yes_means` and `no_means`, `threshold`, `min_confidence` and `fallback`. A top level `assert` or `abstain_if` is the file's gate. An unknown key exits 2 rather than being ignored. An `--ask` beside `-f` adds a question, and reusing an id from the file needs `--replace`. `-f` also takes a request body, a file with a `questions` key such as `--print-request` writes. For one record, a body's own `state` is sent as it is, and stdin is then never read, so `--state` or `--state-file` beside it exits 2. A stream or `calibrate` sends each record as its state and warns that the body's state is ignored. Save a set the repository shares as `.onesie/questions/NAME.yaml`, after `mkdir -p .onesie/questions` since the redirect creates no directory, or one for every project under `questions` in the config dir that holds `profiles.json`, and `-f NAME` finds it. A value with no slash and no dot that is not a file in the working directory is a name, looked up in the nearest `.onesie/questions` at or above the working directory, then in the config dir, as `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json`. A name found nowhere, or with two files in one directory, exits 2 and names the directories. `onesie questions` lists every name with the file it resolves to.

`--cache`, or `ONESIE_CACHE=1` in the environment of every run, stores each successful response on disk and answers a repeated request from it, with no request and zero tokens. A change to the state, the questions, the model, the provider or the base URL asks again, while `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--assert` and the output flags do not. On the `typesafe` provider a model name ending in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on OpenRouter or Berget, so its answers expire after 24 hours, or after `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL`. `--cache=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, so that run asks the API again. Cached answers stay on disk until they expire, are evicted or `onesie cache clear` removes them.

Every output format writes each number of an answer as `-o json` does. A number the provider sent prints as sent, never rounded. A number onesie computes itself, such as `norm` or a mock's `p` and `score`, is rounded to four places. A printed number is the one a gate compares.

A pick or rate answer carries `confidence`, a number from 0 to 1 the API computes from `p`. `--min-confidence` cuts on it. A yes or no answer carries no confidence. A response that leaves `confidence` out reads as 0, so `--min-confidence` falls back and a gate on `confidence` does not pass.

Every answer is checked against the question asked before it is printed, gated or cached, on a plain run, in a stream, under `-q` and `--assert`, in `calibrate` and when the cache is read. A yes or no value, each `p` and each `confidence` lies in [0,1], a pick names one of its options, a rate's `score` lies between 0 and its top level index, the keys of `p` are exactly the options, or the level indexes from 0 for a rate, and `p` adds up to 1 within half a hundredth per entry, and at least a hundredth. An answer of the wrong type fails too. Any of these exits 4 with `200 response could not be used:` and names the question and the value, as in `question 'urgent' answered 1.5, which lies outside [0,1]`. In a stream the record is an error line of kind `response`. Its tokens still count toward `--usage` and `--stats`, it is never stored in the cache, and it is not retried.

A question that is one bare word close to a subcommand name exits 2 and names the closest subcommand, as `onesie questoins` does. A word after `--` is asked, as in `onesie -- questoins`, and so is a question of more than one word or one beside `--ask`.

A file of one line whose object carries a key `-o json` writes on a line, `id`, `line`, `model`, `usage`, `assert`, `abstain` or an `error` object, is the line shape. So the `--out` file of a one record run answers record 1 alone, and record 2 exits 2 with a message naming the key. An object over several lines that carries one of those keys is refused.

A yes or no answer is a probability, or an object whose `value` is one. A pick or rate answer is a name, or an object with `value` and an optional `confidence`, which defaults to 1. With no `p`, onesie fills one in where the value is the most likely and the others share the rest evenly. A rate's `score` is the level index averaged over `p`, unless the entry gives one. A number whose text is a name is that name, so `4` rates `--rate 1,2,3,4,5`. A rate question from a request body takes its level index.

The other keys `-o json` writes are accepted. A line's `model`, `usage`, `line`, `assert` and `abstain` are ignored, since the gate runs again. Inside an answer, `decision`, `fallback` and `legend` are ignored. A rate's `score` and `norm` are replayed, and so is a pick or rate's `p`, whose keys must be exactly the options or levels, whose values lie between 0 and 1 and add up to 1 within 0.02, and whose most likely entry is the value. So a replay prints the answers the real run printed, and a gate that reads `p` decides the same way. The `model` it prints is the one the mock run resolved, not the one the record holds.
Requirements live only on the command line. A question file carries none.

The `-o json` report gains a `require` array, one entry per requirement: `{"expr":"u.catches >= 0.9 at 0.5","held":false,"value":0.6667,"interval":[0.2077,0.9385],"cut":0.5}`, for 2 of 3 caught. A requirement compares the four place number the `-o json` report prints. A rate, interval end or `auc` that is not exactly 0 or 1 never prints as 0 or 1, so 29999 of 30000 is `0.9999`. The table report shows each rate and interval end as a whole percent between 1 and 99, so `1/1000` reads `1% 1-1%` and `4/4` reads `99% 51-99%`, and `auc` to 2 places. `auc` has `"interval":null`, a pick or rate measure `"cut":null`, and a measure over no records `"value":null` with a `reason`.
The starter sets in `examples/` commit their answers files, and `examples/README.md` lists the requirements each one holds.
Use `--map` to drop the fields that do not bear on the question, such as timestamps and ids, since they add noise to the answer. `--map 'del(.ts, .order_id)'` sends the rest of a record.
`line` is not part of the `--out` fingerprint. A resume with `--id` keeps each stored line as written, so a skipped record keeps the line number it was answered at, as it keeps its answer.

`--resume` with `--id` skips answered records and asks the rest, failed ones included. A finished run rewrites the file in input order and keeps answered ids missing from the input, unless `--prune` drops them. A changed fingerprint refuses with exit 2. A record whose content changed but whose id did not keeps its old answer. Without `--id`, it carries on by line count. It does not ask a failed record again, apart from the `--stop-on-error` case below, so a skipped error line still counts as failed toward exit 6 and `--stats`, under `-i request` too. Either way, a skipped record keeps its stored `--assert` outcome, so it counts toward the exit code and `--stats` as if it were judged again.

Records whose request is identical are asked once in a run. Identical means the same state after `--map`, the same questions and the same model, and under `--mock` the same answer from the file. A JSON line's whitespace does not matter, but its key order does. A record the mock file does not answer is never shared. Every record still gets its own line, with its own `id` and its own input under `--merge`, in input order or as answers arrive under `--unordered`. `--stats` counts the saved requests, as in `12 records, 3 deduplicated, 9 requests`. Under `--usage` only the first line written for a request carries its tokens, and its other lines carry `{"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0}`, so a sum over the output stays true. An error line that carried no usage still carries none. A failed request fails every record that shares it, and is not asked again within the run. With `--id`, `--resume` judges each line on its own, so a later run asks those records again. Without `--id` it carries on by line count, which asks no failed record again. A run holds up to `max-dedup-requests` distinct requests, which `onesie -V` lists. Past that it says so once on stderr, still shares the requests it holds and asks every new one. Only a stream deduplicates: calibrate, `-i request` and `--print-request` ask or print every record. `--no-dedup` asks every record.

`-o csv` and `-o tsv` write one column per question, named by its id, then an `assert` column under a gate and an `error` column. A question with a fallback gets an `ID_fallback` column right after its own, as in `team,team_fallback`. It holds `low_confidence` or `error` when the fallback replaced the answer, the same reason `-o json` writes as `fallback`, and is empty otherwise. Under `--merge` the input columns come first, and one named like an output column exits 2. `--resume` refuses a csv or tsv file without the fallback columns, and says to regenerate it or write to a new `--out`.
The cache, deduplication and `--resume` see the same image file as the same record.
A request with an image waits up to 60 seconds per attempt, unless `--timeout` says otherwise. Lower `-j` for large images, since each record in flight holds its image bytes.

`--print-request` writes onesie's request format: the System One body plus the settings that change the answer, each image as base64 under `assets`. `-i request` reads lines up to `max-request-line-bytes`, so a printed body replays. A printed body holding `long_context` is refused by TypeSafe if sent to it directly, rather than through `-i request`.
TypeSafe takes images and Box questions.
OpenRouter takes each image where its reference stands. An image named in several places is sent once per place, and counts toward the body size each time.
Cloudflare takes images and no Box questions. Clef takes up to 4 images, and a question names an image as it does on TypeSafe.
Images and Box are experimental, and less reliable than text.

On the `typesafe` provider, a model name that ends in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned, and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on any other provider, `typesafe/jev-1.13` on OpenRouter and `Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B` on Berget and `levanto-sage-v1.4` on Levanto included. An alias's answers expire after 24 hours, since the model behind it can move. `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` sets that lifetime as a duration, such as `90m` or `72h`, and `0` stops reading and storing answers for an alias. A negative or malformed value exits 2, in every run whether or not it uses the cache, in `onesie cache` and in `onesie cache clear`. A short lifetime in one run never deletes answers other runs still read.

Its files are mode `600` in directories of mode `700`. `--cache` refuses a cache directory others can reach with exit 2, before any request, apart from on Windows. onesie writes a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, so backup tools skip the cache. `--cache` refuses an existing directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` that holds anything else with exit 2, before any request. onesie counts, evicts and clears only its own entries, and parallel runs can share one cache.

`--mock` answers from its file and never reads or fills the cache. `--print-request` sends nothing, `calibrate --offline` asks nothing, and a run that `--resume` finds fully answered asks nothing, so none of them opens the cache. `-i request` and `--list-models` never go through it, so `--cache` beside either exits 2. `--cache=false` beside them is fine, and `ONESIE_CACHE=1` is ignored there.
A cached run still needs a key, even though a hit sends nothing. Under `--cache`, the no key message says so.

`create` and `update` check the rules below, the base URL and the account id before they read the key, so a typo costs nothing. A bad value from a flag is named by its flag, as in `--account-id must be 32 hexadecimal characters`.

An empty or whitespace only variable counts as unset. A flag that names a value, such as a file, a model or a profile, exits 2 on an empty or whitespace only one, so `--mock "$UNSET"` never reaches the API. `profile update` is the exception, where an empty value clears a member.

A question file carries no model, since `model` is a reserved question id there. Only a request body, as `--print-request` writes it, names one. Under `-i request` each body sends the model it names, and a body that names none, or an empty, all whitespace or null one, takes the profile's `model`, then the order above. Only the key `model` spelled in that case counts, so a body that holds only `Model` names none. Of several `model` keys the last one counts, and a blank last one leaves a single `model` key. onesie writes that model into the body, so `--print-request` shows it too.

A key goes to the OS keychain under the service `onesie`: the macOS Keychain, the Secret Service on Linux, or the Windows Credential Manager. The item is named `PROFILE@HASH`, where the hash stands for the config dir, so two config dirs never share one item. The profile's `account` holds the name. A converted profile keeps its item name until `onesie profile update NAME --key`.
`profile delete` and `profile update --key` delete the replaced item after the file is saved, unless another profile names the same item. A failure warns and names the item left behind.
No variable holds the whole file.

An error response whose body is not JSON, such as the HTML page a web server sends for a wrong path, prints its status and says the body is not JSON, as in `onesie: 405 Method Not Allowed, with a response body that is not JSON. Check that the base URL points at the System One API`. A page is left out, and only the first line of a plain text body is kept. Only a 404 or a 405 adds the hint to check the base URL. A body sent as JSON that holds only a string prints the first line of that string after the status.

`-f VALUE` reads VALUE as a file when one exists at that path. Otherwise a bare name loads `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json` from the nearest `.onesie/questions`, then from `questions` in the config dir, and last takes a starter set built into onesie: `moderation`, `personal-data`, `prompt-injection` or `shell-safety`. A saved file wins over a built-in set of the same name, so a copy to edit is printed elsewhere first, as in `onesie -f shell-safety --print-questions > shell-safety.yaml`, then moved with `mv shell-safety.yaml .onesie/questions/`. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions` empties the file before onesie runs, and `-f` then finds that empty file ahead of the built-in set. `onesie questions` lists every name `-f` finds, with a built-in set shown as `built in` and an empty saved file marked `empty`, or `"empty":true` under `-o json`. A question file is refused with exit 2 when it uses a YAML alias or when it is larger than `max-question-file-bytes`, and every error in a file names its path. A file that holds no question, such as an empty one, `{}` or only comments, adds nothing beside `--ask`, and on its own it exits 2, naming the file. One that hides a built-in set always exits 2, naming how to reach the set.

`-f` also takes a request body, as `--print-request` writes it, a positional question's body keyed `answer` included. For one record, a body that holds a `state` sends that state, and onesie then never reads stdin. `--state` or `--state-file` beside such a body exits 2, naming both. `-i request` refuses both flags the same way, since each body there holds its own state. A stream and `calibrate` read their records from stdin as usual and send each one as its state, so they use the body only for its questions, and say on stderr that its state is ignored. A body's `assets` are sent with it. When its state is ignored, an asset only that state named is dropped, and the warning counts it.

`--print-schema` prints the JSON Schema for a question file. The first line `--print-questions` writes is `# yaml-language-server: $schema=URL`, which an editor running the YAML language server reads, such as VS Code with the Red Hat YAML extension, to check each key and value as you type. The URL names the release tag the binary was built from, and `main` for any other build. A JSON question file names the schema in a top level `"$schema"` key, which onesie accepts and ignores, so `$schema` is a reserved question id. The schema accepts any request body as it is.

An editor flags a `threshold` outside 0 to 1 or a pick with one option. It accepts a file that holds only a gate, an `abstain_if` with no `assert`, or a `min_confidence` with no `fallback`, since a flag can supply the rest, and onesie refuses such a file at run time when the flag is missing.

`--long-context`, or `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, raises the context limits to 262k tokens, which is slower and less accurate. It is written into a printed body as `long_context`, so a replay keeps it, and a `-f` body's `long_context: true` turns it on with no flag. A body's `false` does not turn off the flag or the variable. The flag wins over the variable, so `--long-context=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, as `--cache=false` does for the cache. It does not turn off a body's `long_context: true`, from `-f` or under `-i request`, since the body asks for it itself. Set that key to `false` in the body, or remove it, to run without it. `-i request` follows the same order for each body it replays, and under `--print-request` it writes `"long_context":true` into a body the flag or the variable turns it on for. A provider that takes no long context refuses the run with exit 2, and when `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT` turned it on, the message says so. It is experimental.

`onesie --help` lists every flag, and `onesie -V` prints the built in limits. A flag onesie does not know exits 2, naming the closest one when one is near. A flag that belongs to a run, given to a subcommand, says so. `-V` takes no question, so a word beside it exits 2. `onesie help calibrate` prints a subcommand's help, and a topic that names no subcommand exits 2.
CheckAll reports the first answer in result that does not fit its question, as Normalize would.
NormalizeAll normalizes the answer to every question, in question order.
Unusable is a 200 response onesie could not use. It has kind response in a stream and exits 4 in a single shot run, since the same request would only get it again.
SumFits reports a distribution's sum, rounded to four places, and whether it is 1 within 0.02.
A provider that writes two places per entry leaves the sum a hundredth or two off 1.
A cache others can read, or a directory that may not be onesie's, is something the user asked for and has to fix, so each ends the run. Any other failure only turns the cache off.
An entry that fails the answer checks would fail every run until it expires, so it is passed over and replaced by a fresh answer.
Ahead of the keychain and of New, so a base URL that carries a key is refused in onesie's words and nothing is sent.
Read only here, so a run that names its provider and has its key never opens the file. An error reading it leaves the hint out, since the missing key is the failure to report.
A file with no question beside --ask only adds nothing, unless it hides the built-in set the user meant to add.
The prepared body names the model onesie sent, and nothing inside it was checked locally, so no local bound is implicated.
The usage is read apart from the answers, so a 200 whose answers onesie cannot read still reports what it cost.
The result holds the same usage, so it fails too, and onesie-go words the failure.
qfile.Load reads a body with no questions key as a bare question map, so the key is looked for first.
Cobra would add completion only when the tree runs, too late to set its argument check.
Every short name sits one or two edits from many unrelated words, so only a longer name earns a second edit.
A flag that asks no question would be refused on a run too.
A flag given is a choice made, so an empty value is refused rather than read as unset. An unset variable in a script would otherwise drop a --mock and send a paid request.
Cost is the summed cost the provider reported, nil when it reported none.

At least twice what each other name takes keeps the value the strict mode, which replayed demands of a written p, since a rate reads its value from the first of equal modes. Rounded up to four places, so the value's p is never below its confidence. The small allowance keeps float noise, as in 0.6 times 10000, from rounding up a whole step.
Package num writes and rounds the numbers onesie prints, so every output mode shows the same one.
Format writes a number as -o json does, in the shortest form that reads back as the same number and never rounded, so every output mode shows the number a gate compares.
Package patherr strips the operation and path an *fs.PathError carries, for a message that names the path itself.
Inner returns the error inside a *fs.PathError, and any other error as it is.
An empty file, or one of only comments, decodes as null and holds no question.
A run refuses a malformed account, so show refuses it too. A missing account prints as none and exits 2 below.
--print-request needs the resolution too, to print the model a body with none is sent with.
Cobra adds the completion command inside Execute. Adding it here lets its argument check be set.
Mkdir respects the umask, so the mode is set explicitly.
Library errors carry the prefix and the CLI's own errors do not, and a consumer filtering stderr should not have to know which layer produced a line.
CheckState rejects a state the API would refuse or the model cannot answer, so a caller holding a state that never passed through Resolve can still check it.
A dry run is left to the flag rules, whose message drops --resume rather than asking for an --id it would then refuse as well.
A resume is left to the flag rules, whose message names --resume as the flag with nothing to do.
A dry run is left to the flag rules, whose message names --print-request as the reason.
DryRunRules returns the command tree, then by long name the flags both dry runs refuse and the ones only --print-questions refuses, so a tool that builds a dry run knows what to strip.
Ahead of checkSingle, so a streaming -q reports the streaming message rather than the single question policy one.
Ahead of the request mode rules, so a flag both of them reject is reported against --list-models, which is the flag that made the mode meaningless.
Both ahead of the output and streaming rules, so a dry run is rejected before anything it would have written reaches stdout.
After the streaming rules, so --stop-on-assert on one record is told it needs a stream first.

A dry run forwards nothing, writes no response body and makes no request, which is what every output facing reason in the request mode table claims. Its own message is the true one here, so it answers first.
Otherwise the request mode rules lead, so a flag -i request rejects outright is named by the message that says so rather than by a general one that happens to fire first.
Every group flag at once, since a listing has no use for any of them and the only part of the message that varies is the name the user typed.
In a fixed order, for the same reason checkRequestMode is.
In a fixed order, so a command line with several offenders reports a predictable one rather than whichever check happened to be written first.

A flag that would quietly do nothing is rejected, and a dry run accepts none of these. In a fixed order, for the same reason checkListModels is. The rules gated on printQuestions are the ones --print-request genuinely consumes.

Guarded to --print-request, since --print-questions writes the assertion into the file it prints and so is the one dry run that carries it. A gate that only the file carries is ignored, so a gated file can be dry run as it stands.
--stop-on-error and --unordered are absent because streamRequests honours both. Only the assertion is a judgment a dry run never makes, so only its stop condition is rejected.
Checked for every mode, since --merge applies to the non streaming ones too.

Also for every mode. The rule is rejected rather than clamped, and a typo in a shared alias is exactly as wrong outside a stream as inside one. Gated on jobsSet because jobs is an int and its zero value cannot be told from the flag being absent.
Zero would have to mean either never honour the header or honour it without bound, so it is rejected rather than given one of those meanings.

The flag the user actually typed and the mode they actually gave. Naming --state for a --state-file mistake sends them to the wrong flag, and naming jsonl for a lines run sends them to the wrong mode.
A stream writes one line per input line. A table is several lines with a repeated header, and unlike raw it has no streaming form.
