Seconds become a time.Duration downstream, and past a point that multiplication wraps. A wrap to a positive value would hand a user who asked for centuries a fraction of a second.
auto resolves to json under a merge, so an explicit auto is as mergeable as an absent flag. The other -o rejections deliberately fire on auto, since a mode they ignore does nothing there.
A resource hint rather than a semantic one, and it may reasonably come from a shared alias, so it warns and proceeds rather than failing.
Both spellings of the raw mode take a single question. Only the -r spelling is exclusive with -o, which is why the two are still distinguished above.
Beside an assertion -q only silences the output, since the assertion is the gate.
The request mode reason is untrue once --print-request is set, since nothing is forwarded and no request is made.
Same, and there is no response body to carry a usage object either.
Once, not twice. checkFlags has two callers, and a run that reached both would report the same warning to the same stream twice.
--input's default is text, so a rejection here can only come from Changed, not from the value differing from the default.
--jobs's default is 1, for the same reason as the --input case above.
Its own rule rather than the -o one, since run leaves Output empty for a bare -r.
The path that returns before a plan is built, so the rule has to sit above it.
Rejected before anything reaches stdout, which is the reason the rule lives in checkFlags rather than in the print path.
A passing case that warns is a rule firing where no rule was expected. A failing one is allowed to carry whatever the checks reached before the fatal error.
The only hint is -j on one record, which --list-models refuses and -i request never is.
Validate checks the questions of a plan and returns the non fatal warnings plus the first fatal error. fileName is the -f value a body policy refusal names.

NewCatalog reads each flag in the command tree under root, its spellings and whether it takes a value. always and questionsOnly name the flags a dry run refuses, which only the caller's flag rules know.
Catalog knows how each flag of a onesie command tree is spelled, so it can turn a command into its dry run.
A second line of defence that never fires today. It goes false only if stripFlags stops dropping a value with its flag, or insertFlag stops leading with the mode flag.
checkFlags runs first, so a streaming -q reports the streaming message.
checkFlags has two callers, and a run that reaches both prints the warning once.
The exit code already says a record failed, and the per record lines on stdout carry the detail.
A rejection is carried by the exit code alone. Under -q nothing is printed at all, and a false assertion has already printed the record.

A 2xx body onesie cannot use is a server fault, not a usage error, so it exits 4 and is never retried. Its kind is response, since http would name a status worth retrying and transport a connection blip that never happened.
A connection that broke with EPIPE exits as the transport failure it is, and stays quiet as every broken pipe does.

After the transport checks, so a socket write that failed with EPIPE keeps the transport exit code. What reaches here is onesie's own stdout, and no exit code means the consumer stopped reading. A line about it would go to a stderr the same consumer is often reading.
The command already wrote the whole result to stdout, so a stderr line would repeat it.

No status arrived and the network did not fail, so the record never became a request, as with a line onesie could not read. Calling it transport would blame the network, and exit 5 where a fresh run exits 2.

--print-request is why this is not folded into the early return --print-questions takes. It includes any state supplied, so it goes through input.Resolve and needs a question only body when nothing was.
The options clientBuilder adds ahead of these, so the order is the one a real run builds.
encoding/json matches a member to a field whatever its case, so a member it would read is a known one.
A syntax error can quote a character of the file, which may be part of a key, so only a member of the wrong type, which names the member and not its value, is passed on.
The kinds a record's error key names.
KindResponse is a 2xx response onesie could not use.
KindHTTP is a response with a status outside 2xx.
KindTransport is a connection that failed or timed out.
KindInput is a record that never became a request.
Kind names what failed, so a consumer can tell a retry worth making from a record to fix.
Package answersfile opens, locks, resumes and compacts the file a run writes its answers to.
The reasons a StaleAnswersError gives for refusing a file.
ErrStaleAnswers matches every StaleAnswersError, so a caller tells a stale file apart without reading the message.
ErrNoLock refuses a resume on a platform with no file lock.
Open resolves and locks the answers file at config.Path and reads what a resume skips. When an error comes after the lock, the File comes back still locked for the caller to release.
Options holds what Open reaches the filesystem through. A nil function or an empty GOOS takes the real one.
Config names the answers file and says how a resume reads it.
Resume says how many records a resume by position skips, the verdicts stored for them and whether the file has its header row.
NotRegularError refuses to resume from a device or a pipe, which holds no answers to read back.
Error names the file.
DirectoryError refuses a path that names a directory.
Error names the directory.
File is the answers file of one run, written through Write and compacted by Finish.
Release lets go of the lock. It is safe on a nil File and after an earlier Release.
Offset is the length of the file as this run has written it.
CompactInto has Finish rewrite the file with these lines in this order.
Write appends to the file, opening it on the first write.
Finish closes the file once the run ended with runErr, and compacts it when CompactInto asked.
Bind checks a resumed file against the run's fingerprint and probes that the file can be written.
BindWithoutFingerprint lets a fresh run write a file that keeps no fingerprint.
Resuming reports whether the run resumes into this file.
StoredFingerprint reads the fingerprint beside a file that holds answers. found is false when either is missing.
StaleAnswersError refuses a file whose fingerprint does not match the run. Sidecar is the file the fingerprint is kept in.
StaleReason says why a file's fingerprint does not match the run.
Error says why the file does not match, without the sentinel's own text.
Cause says why the file does not match, in words that follow since.
Fingerprint sums the questions, the form they are sent in and the inputs that change an answer.
FingerprintInputs are the choices beside the questions that Fingerprint covers.
ResumeLedger reads the answers a resume by id skips. It is nil when the run does not resume by id.
ResumedVerdicts reads the verdict on each line a resume by position skips. Under stopOnError a stored failure on the last line is asked again.
ReadSpans calls read with the text of each span, reading the file forward. The text is reused across calls.
In file order, so the reads move forward through the file.
Format says how the answers were written, so a resume reads them back.
Verdict is a stored line's outcome: rejected by the gate, abstained or failed.
Span is a line's byte range in the answers file.
Ledger keys the answered lines of a resume by id, and orders the lines for compaction.
Admit gives a record its slot in the order, and its stored verdict when the file answers it.
StoredAt is where the file answers id, when it does.
Keep puts the line answering id in the order without asking it again.
Kept in its place and nothing more. The record is not asked, so it is neither pending nor skipped.
Forget drops the line answering id, so its record is asked again.
Wrote records where the line for slot was written.
End marks the input as read to its end.
Complete reports whether every record was read and every line written.
TakeOrder hands over the lines in input order. Without prune the lines no record asked for follow.
Skipped counts the records a resume skipped.
Tally counts records and their outcomes.
Count adds one record with this verdict.
The kinds of Notice.
SaveWarning is a failure after the profiles file was written that did not stop the write, in Err.
KeyInKeychain means the key went into the keychain item Account.
KeyInFile means the keychain refused the key with Err, so it went into the profiles file.
FirstDefault means the profile created became the default, as the first profile.
DefaultDeleted means the profile deleted was the default, so no profile is the default now.
ItemLeftBehind means the keychain item Account could not be removed, for Err.
OldKeyUnread means the keychain item Account holds the new key, and its old key could not be read to put back.
OldKeyLost means Err kept the old key from going back into the keychain item Account, which holds the new key.
NewProfileManager builds a ProfileManager that writes profiles through store and keeps their keys in keychain.
ProfileManager creates, updates and deletes profiles, keeping profiles.json and the keychain items in step. Each change returns notices for the user, also beside an error.
Create stores a new profile and its key, in the keychain unless ToFile says the file. The first profile becomes the default.
Update writes the changed profile. With ReadKey it replaces the key too, and puts the old key back when the file cannot be written.
Delete removes the named profile, then its keychain item unless another profile names it. Deleting the last profile removes the file.
Change names one profile in the profiles file at Path, which holds Profiles now. ReadKey reads the new key, Update keeps the key when ReadKey is nil, and Delete needs no Profile, ToFile or ReadKey.
Notice is one thing a profile change tells the user beside its outcome. Kind says what, and Account and Err fill it in.
NoticeKind names what a Notice reports.
With returns a copy of the profiles that holds profile under name.
QuotedName quotes a name in a message, such as a profile, a provider or a member of profiles.json.

`-o markdown`, or `-o md`, writes a stream as one GitHub table with a summary alert. A table cannot be read back into answers, so `--resume`, `--merge`, `-r` and `-q` exit 2. Read answers with `-o json` or `-o csv`. A GitHub comment holds at most 65536 characters, so send a large stream to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` or write it as csv. The rest is under Streams in [REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#streams).

`--map EXPR` is a jq expression whose result is the state, so `--map '.body'` keeps a customer name away from the model. Drop every field that does not bear on the question, such as a timestamp or an order id, since each one adds noise to the answer. `--id EXPR` names each record on every output line, and `--resume` skips by it. Keep it a cheap field lookup that yields one string or number, unique per record. A record whose map or id fails gets an error line, and the stream carries on. The rest is under Streams in [REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#streams).

Pass `--resume` from the first run, since a missing or empty `--out` file starts fresh. After a failure, rerun with the same `--out` and `--id`: the run skips every id the file answers and asks the rest, failed records included. `-j`, `--timeout` and `--retries` may change between runs. Exit 2 means the questions, flags or gate changed, so drop `--resume` and start over. A record whose content changed under the same id keeps its old answer. The rest is under Streams in [REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#streams). A full resume: `onesie 'is this urgent' -i jsonl -j 8 --map '.body' --id '.id' --out answers.jsonl --resume < tickets.jsonl`.

`--print-questions > q.yaml` writes the questions, their policy flags and any assertion as YAML, and `onesie -f q.yaml` reads it back. Save a set the repository shares as `.onesie/questions/NAME.yaml`, after `mkdir -p .onesie/questions`, and `-f NAME` finds it. An `--ask` beside `-f` adds a question, and reusing an id from the file needs `--replace`. An unknown key exits 2. `onesie questions` lists every name with the file it resolves to. The lookup order and the file format are under More in [REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#more).
A resume with `--id` keeps each stored line as written, so a skipped record keeps the line number it was answered at, as it keeps its answer.
`--out` writes to a file with a fingerprint beside it, and a lock so two runs cannot share it.

`--resume` refuses with exit 2 when a change would alter what a record is asked or what its line holds: the questions or their policy flags, the provider, the model, the images, long context, `--mock`, the input or output format, `--map`, `--id`, `--merge-key`, `--assert` or `--abstain-if`. `--skip-blank` counts too when a resume counts lines, which is without `--id` on any input but csv and tsv. A file written by another onesie version is refused the same way. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.

`--resume` with `--id` skips answered records and asks the rest, failed ones included. A finished run rewrites the file in input order and keeps answered ids missing from the input, unless `--prune` drops them. A record whose content changed but whose id did not keeps its old answer. Without `--id`, it carries on by line count. It does not ask a failed record again, apart from the `--stop-on-error` case below, so a skipped error line still counts as failed toward exit 6 and `--stats`, under `-i request` too. Either way, a skipped record keeps its stored `--assert` outcome, so it counts toward the exit code and `--stats` as if it were judged again.

Under `--stop-on-assert`, a skipped false assertion ends the run where a fresh run would stop. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume by line count whose last line is an error line drops that line, asks its record again and carries on. A run stopped by `--stop-on-error` leaves exactly that, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it was written without `--stop-on-error`, so the resume stops there before any request and exits with the failed record's own code, as a fresh run under `--stop-on-error` would. A csv or tsv row keeps only the message, so there it exits 2. Either way, pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. The same holds under `-i request`. With `--id` the failed record is asked again, and stops the run only if it fails again.

A stored answer is used only for the same request. A change to the state, the questions, the model, long context, the provider, the base URL or any image asks the API again. `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--assert`, `--abstain-if`, the policy flags and the output flags never change the answer, so a run that differs only in those still hits.

Deduplication covers repeats within one run, the cache covers repeats across runs, and `--resume` skips the ids an `--out` file already answers. A group of identical records asks the cache once, so a group whose first record hits counts one cached record and the rest deduplicated. A cached line in `--out` carries zero usage like any other hit. Turning the cache on or off never refuses a resume, so a file written with the cache resumes without it, and the other way round. `calibrate --cache` works too.

`--box` makes a question a box, answered with `left`, `top`, `right` and `bottom`, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner, and a `confidence`. It needs an image, as in Images below, and a provider that takes it, TypeSafe or OpenRouter, as on `typesafe/jev-1.14`. Cloudflare, Levanto and Berget refuse it before any request. On TypeSafe and OpenRouter the model must serve it too: one that does not answers 400 `Invalid request`, and onesie then names `-m jev-preview`, which does. It takes no value and no `--desc`, `--threshold`, `--min-confidence` or `--fallback`. `-r` prints the four edges in that order, and `-o csv` writes them as four columns, `ID_left`, `ID_top`, `ID_right` and `ID_bottom`. A box always returns a box, even when the target is not there, so pair it with a yes or no question that asks whether it is.

A request with an image waits up to 60 seconds per attempt, unless `--timeout` says otherwise. `onesie -V` lists it as `asset-attempt-timeout`, beside `attempt-timeout`. Lower `-j` for large images, since each record in flight holds its image bytes.

Under `-i request` onesie fills a blank `model` and checks each body as a send would, before it sends anything: the provider must take what the body asks for, each image must pass the image limits, `long_context` must be true or false, and no question may pass `max-choice-options` or `max-score-levels`. A body that fails is an error line of kind `input`, and nothing is sent for it. `--print-request` refuses the same bodies with the same error lines. It also checks each 200 that comes back before printing it. A response that is not JSON, that is not a System One result with an `answers` object, or whose answers do not decode, is an error line of kind `response` with `200 response could not be used:`, and the run exits 6. When the body's `questions` read as a `-f` body's would, each answer is also checked against its question as on any other run, so a missing answer or a value out of its range fails the same way. A body whose questions onesie cannot read, such as one past `max-question-file-bytes`, gets only the first checks. The tokens of a refused response still count toward `--stats`.

`show` never reads the keychain or prints a key. `key:` is `keychain` or `file`, with `, ends in XXXX` when the key has 16 characters or more, `env` and the key variable for a run without a profile, or `none`. A converted keychain key shows no ending until `onesie profile update NAME --key`. `chosen by:` is `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE`, `the default`, `--provider`, `ONESIE_PROVIDER` or `nothing`, and `not active` for a named profile a run would not use. `model:` and `base_url:` give the value a run would use, in the order a run picks it, then where it comes from. The model comes from `profile`, `env TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` or `the provider's default`, as in `model: jev-latest, the provider's default`. The base URL comes from `the profile's base_url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, `the profile's account_id`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `the provider's default`, the words a run's messages use. `base_url:` is `none` on cloudflare with no account, and a base URL a run would refuse exits 2 with the run's message. An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters.

On cloudflare the account counts only when no base URL is chosen, since a Cloudflare base URL holds the account. A profile's `account_id` comes right after `--base-url` and the profile's `base_url`, so it beats every variable, and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` comes after them. A cloudflare run with no account exits 2 and names `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`. On a profile it also names `onesie profile update NAME --account-id ACCOUNT_ID`, and without one `onesie profile create NAME --provider cloudflare --account-id ACCOUNT_ID`.

An error response whose body is not JSON, such as the HTML page a web server sends for a wrong path, prints its status and says the body is not JSON, as in `onesie: 405 Method Not Allowed, with a response body that is not JSON. Check that the base URL points at the System One API`. A page is left out, and only the first line of a plain text body is kept. Only a 404 or a 405 adds the hint to check the base URL. A body sent as JSON that holds only a string is read as a plain text body is: its first line is kept, a page is left out, and an empty one prints the status text.

A base URL that holds a user or a password, or any `@`, `?` or `#`, or that does not parse, exits 2 before any request, whether it comes from `--base-url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` or a profile, so a key never travels in a URL or reaches a message. So does one with no host or with a scheme other than http or https. The message names where the URL came from, `--base-url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` or `the profile's base_url`, and shows at most its scheme and host, as in `onesie: --base-url https:// names no host`. `profile create` and `profile update` refuse one too, and `profile show` refuses a profile that holds one. `--print-request` sends nothing and does not check it.

`--long-context`, or `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, raises the context limits to 262k tokens, which is slower and less accurate. It is written into a printed body as `long_context`, so a replay keeps it, and a `-f` body's `long_context: true` turns it on with no flag. A body's `false` does not turn off the flag or the variable. The flag wins over the variable, so `--long-context=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT=1`, as `--cache=false` does for the cache. It does not turn off a body's `long_context: true`, from `-f` or under `-i request`, since the body asks for it itself. UnusableError is an answer that came back but cannot be used. A record gets kind response and a single shot run exits 4.

There are two ways in. A user who installs onesie first can add the plugin afterwards. A user who installs the plugin first gets a session start line saying onesie is missing or has no key, and this skill takes it from there.

The install script, `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/main/install.sh | sh`. It checks the sha256 of the download, installs to `~/.local/bin` or to `$ONESIE_INSTALL_DIR`, and warns when that directory is not on PATH.

A Go toolchain, at the version `go.mod` names or newer, with `go install github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/cmd/onesie@latest`. It writes the binary to `$GOBIN`, or to `$(go env GOPATH)/bin` when that is unset, which is often not on PATH. If `command -v onesie` still finds nothing, have the user add that directory to PATH in their shell profile and open a new shell.
Prefer these three to a download from the releases page, which leaves the user to unpack the archive and put the binary on PATH by hand.

A name in place of `work` is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits, `-` or `_`, does not start with `-`, and is not `none`. A profile holds the provider, its key, and optionally `--model`, the model a run uses when it names none, and `--base-url`, or `--account-id` on cloudflare. The first profile becomes the default, and `onesie profile use NAME` changes it. [Choosing a profile][choosing] gives the order a run picks a profile in. `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` runs without a profile and reads only the provider's env var, which suits CI.

Profiles live in `profiles.json`, in the config dir [profiles.json][file] names. The file is written at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in the file itself. An older `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item.

The plugin adds the onesie skills and a session start line that reports whether onesie is on PATH, whether a key resolves, whether `onesie --version` differs from the release the skills describe, and which question files `-f` finds. It never blocks a command.

`--cache`, or `ONESIE_CACHE=1` in the environment of every run, stores each successful response on disk and answers a repeated request from it, with no request and zero tokens. A change to the state, the questions, the model, the provider or the base URL asks again, while `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--assert` and the output flags do not. On the `typesafe` provider a model name ending in a version, such as `jev-1.13.0`, is pinned and its answers live until they are evicted. Every other model is an alias, such as `jev-latest`, and so is every model on any other provider, as [Caching](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#caching) lists, so its answers expire after 24 hours, or after `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL`. `--cache=false` turns it off for one run under `ONESIE_CACHE=1`, so that run asks the API again. Cached answers stay on disk until they expire, are evicted or `onesie cache clear` removes them.

A profile, stored with `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER`, holds a provider, its key and optionally a model. A run picks its profile in the order [Choosing a profile](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#choosing-a-profile) gives, and a profile's key and model beat the provider's variables. `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` runs without a profile on that provider. typesafe is the default provider and reads `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, plus `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` and `TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` when they are set. openrouter reads `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone, and never falls back to the TypeSafe key or those two variables. `jev-latest` works on both, but a pinned model id does not carry over: TypeSafe pins `jev-1.13.0`, OpenRouter pins `typesafe/jev-1.13`. berget reads `BERGET_API_KEY` alone and serves its own models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` names the rest. levanto reads `LEVANTO_API_KEY` alone and serves its Sage models, not `jev-latest`: its default is the `sage-latest` alias. cloudflare reads `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, defaults to `typesafe/jev` through AI Gateway, which needs credits, and serves `clef`, `clef-flash` and `clef-omni`. It takes images but no Box or long context. `onesie profile show` names the profile, the provider and where the key lives.
The [exit code table](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#exit-codes) gives each code by outcome, and `onesie --help` lists the same table.

A run uses one profile, or none. [Choosing a profile][choosing] gives the order a run picks it in, [What a run uses][uses] where the key, the model and the base URL come from, and [profiles.json][file] where the file lives. No provider falls back to another's key.
A refused key, where the message names `onesie profile update NAME --key` on a profile run, and the provider's key variable on a run without a profile.
An account out of credits.

`go.mod` names the Go version, `make` lists every target, and `golangci-lint` is expected on `PATH` at the version `.github/workflows/ci.yml` pins. [MAINTAINING.md](MAINTAINING.md) covers the layout, the live suite, the calibrated gates and releases.
In the Apple Developer account, create a Developer ID Application certificate on the `G2 Sub-CA` from that request.
**Wire the gate into a script.** Exit 0 runs the command, 1 blocks it and 7 asks a person. Any other exit code means there was no answer, as the [exit code table](REFERENCE.md#exit-codes) says.

**Rank records by several questions.** One `--ask` per dimension scores every record, and `jq` weighs the answers and sorts by the sum. `.value` is the yes or no probability, and `.norm` is the rate's position between 0 and 1. The weighting lives in `jq`, since `--assert` has no arithmetic, and `select(has("error") | not)` drops the records that failed.

The file takes one of two shapes. One JSON object keyed by question id answers every record, as in `{"destroys": 0.93, "secrets": 0.02, "network": 0.1}`, and may span several lines. A positional question has the id `answer`. Otherwise each line is one entry in the shape `-o json` writes, so the `--out` file of a real run replays. Lines match records by `id` under `--id`, and by position otherwise, so line 3 answers the third record whatever input line it came from. Blank lines are refused, apart from those at the end.

`{"error": N}` with a status from 400 to 599 fails the record as that status does, `{"error": "timeout"}` as a timeout after `--timeout`, and `{"error": "connection"}` as a transport failure. An error object as `-o json` writes it replays by its `kind`. For one record, a 401, 402 or 403 exits 3, a 5xx exits 4 and a timeout exits 5. In a stream a failed record is an error line and the run exits 6, apart from a 401, 402 or 403, which ends it with exit 3.

A requirement reads `[lower|upper](ID.MEASURE) OP NUMBER [at CUT]`. `MEASURE` is `catches`, `false_alarms`, `right_when_flagged` or `auc` for a yes or no question, `agreement` for pick and rate, and `within_one` for rate. `OP` is `>=`, `>`, `<=` or `<`. `NUMBER` and `CUT` are fractions between 0 and 1, so `95` exits 2 with `write 0.95, not 95`.

A yes or no measure other than `auc` is read at one cut. `at CUT` names it, and `at abstain` takes it from the `-f` file's `abstain_if`. Without `at`, the file's `assert` gives it, when it compares the question as `ID.value < X` or `ID.value >= X`. A gate that compares the question with `>` or `<=`, through a function such as `max()`, through `in`, or at two different cuts gives none, and the requirement then needs `at`. A missing cut exits 2 before any request, naming the question.

A run `--stop-on-error` ends exits with the failed record's own code, as in [Exit codes](#exit-codes). A record that never became a request, such as a line onesie could not read or an empty state, has no code of its own, so it exits 6 as it does without the flag, and its error line is the only report.

Under `-i lines`, each `-o json` and `-o values` line carries `line`, the record's input line number from 1. A blank line `--skip-blank` drops still counts, so the numbers match the file. Under `--merge` it sits in the answers object, beside `model`. `-o csv`, `-o tsv`, `-o markdown` and raw output leave it out, and `line` is a reserved question id under `-i lines`.

`onesie cache` prints how many entries the cache holds, how many of them expire since their model is an alias, their size and the directory, or `0 entries in DIR` when there is none. It creates nothing, and names a directory others can reach on stderr. `onesie cache clear` removes every entry, keeps the directory and its `CACHEDIR.TAG`, and prints how many it removed. It refuses a directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` with exit 2, so a mistyped `ONESIE_CACHE_DIR` never empties a directory onesie did not make. Both ignore `--mock` and `ONESIE_CACHE`. A one word question `cache` needs `--ask`, or `--` before it.

A key the server refuses exits 3, on a run or on `test`. On a profile the message names `onesie profile update NAME --key`, and without one it names the provider's key variable. A run with no key and no profile for its provider names `onesie profile create NAME --provider PROVIDER`.
A request body that names no model takes the profile's `model`, then the order above.

`jev-latest` works on typesafe and openrouter, but pinned ids differ: `jev-1.13.0` on TypeSafe, `typesafe/jev-1.13` on OpenRouter. Berget serves its own models and not `jev-latest`. Its default is the `systemone` alias, and `--list-models` there lists only the System One models, each with its aliases. Levanto also serves its own models and not `jev-latest`. Its default is the `sage-latest` alias. On OpenRouter, `--usage` also reports the cost, which the `-o table` header and `--stats` show too. A 200 whose answers onesie cannot use still spent its tokens, so under `--usage` its json error record carries them too, and `--stats` counts them. `-o values`, `-o raw`, `-r`, `-o csv` and `-o tsv` have no place for `--usage`, and `-q` writes nothing, so they all refuse it with exit 2.

A plain `http://` base URL to a host other than this machine exits 2 before any request, since the key would cross the network unencrypted. `--allow-http` sends it anyway, with a warning. The rule holds whether the URL comes from `--base-url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` or a profile's `base_url`, and `profile test` follows it too. `profile create` and `profile update` refuse such a `--base-url` unless given `--allow-http`, and the file does not record that choice, so every run on the profile needs `--allow-http` as well, and `profile show` prints `allow_http: needed`. There is no variable for it.

`-f VALUE` reads VALUE as a file when one exists at that path. Otherwise a bare name loads `NAME.yaml`, `NAME.yml` or `NAME.json` from the nearest `.onesie/questions`, then from `questions` in the config dir, and last takes a starter set built into onesie: `moderation`, `personal-data`, `prompt-injection` or `shell-safety`. A saved file wins over a built in set of the same name, so a copy to edit is printed elsewhere first, as in `onesie -f shell-safety --print-questions > shell-safety.yaml`, then moved with `mv shell-safety.yaml .onesie/questions/`. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions` empties the file before onesie runs, and `-f` then finds that empty file ahead of the built in set. `onesie questions` lists every name `-f` finds, with a built in set shown as `built in` and an empty saved file marked `empty`, or `"empty":true` under `-o json`. A question file is refused with exit 2 when it uses a YAML alias or when it is larger than `max-question-file-bytes`, and every error in a file names its path. A file that holds no question, such as an empty one, `{}` or only comments, adds nothing beside `--ask`, and on its own it exits 2, naming the file. One that hides a built in set always exits 2, naming how to reach the set.
Command skillcheck dry runs every rule's bad and good example under skills/, checks the flags and commands the prose names against onesie --help, and checks the punctuation of the docs.

To edit a set, save a copy into `.onesie/questions/`. A saved file wins over the built in set of the same name, so print the copy elsewhere and move it in. A redirect straight into `.onesie/questions/` would empty the file before `-f` read it:
Names lists the built in sets in name order.
Read returns the built in set a name gives, and false when there is none.
Answer is the normalized shape for one question. Absent fields are omitted, which is what makes a yes or no answer a bare value, not a mostly empty object.
A yes or no decision stays boolean whether it came from a threshold or from a fallback, so a consumer can branch on the JSON type without knowing which produced it.
Both sides of the min_confidence branch in answer.Apply, so a decision is read back whether the model's answer stood or the fallback replaced it.
Both sides of the min_confidence branch in answer.Apply on 'team', where decision names the fallback exactly when it fired and fallback says why.
WriteJSON renders the report as one json object on one line. It holds every row the table shows, plus a yes or no row at every distinct value, the whole grid and every miss.
Label is one record's right answer for one question. Yes holds a yes or no label and Name holds a pick or rate label.
ShapeName is a shape as the header of a report names it.
At is the cut a yes or no requirement reads, named by a number or taken from the file's abstain_if. Value is set only for AtNumber.
Check measures the requirement against one question's score, reading a yes or no measure at cut. A measure over no records, or at a cut the score has no row for, does not hold.
The measures a requirement can read. The first four are yes or no measures, agreement is pick and rate, and within_one is rate.
YesNo reports whether the measure reads a yes or no question.
NeedsCut reports whether the measure is read at one cut, which every yes or no measure but auc is.
ScoreYesNo scores yes or no answers, whose values lie in [0,1], against their labels. A record is flagged at a cut when its value is at or above the cut, and failed counts failed requests.
YesNoScore is how well a yes or no question's answers agree with its labels. Values holds a row at every distinct value answered, and Misses every case past the middle, widest gap first.
YesNoCase is one answered record of a yes or no question, with its label and the value answered. ID is nil when the run has no --id, and Line is the record's input line.
ExitUsage means a usage or validation error, or a 4xx response no other exit code claims.
The probabilities must come back keyed by the labels this invocation supplied, not by the API's own index strings. Keying by label is the whole reason labels exist and no stub can prove it.
A labelled question keys the probabilities by its own labels and drops the legend, which is the opposite of the body case below.
A file with no question beside --ask only adds nothing, unless it hides the built in set the user meant to add.

options wires the tree through the public options where they exist, so the command tree resolves the config dir from the environment as it does in production. It turns the built in sets off, so a test sees only the files it names.
Path is nil for a built in set, which has no file.
The ordered bytes the loader kept, not a Go map marshalled again, so the body reaches the wire in the order it was written.
The threshold defaults to a half, so a yes or no question is meaningful under -q with no policy at all, unlike a pick question which has nothing to compare.
Package limits holds the constants --version reports.

The shape is only final once the loop ends, and a yes or no fallback has to be a boolean by the time anything reads it, whether or not validation ran. Unparseable text is reported by checkPolicy, which owns the user facing message.
Boolean is the parsed value for a yes or no question, where decision stays boolean.
ParseFallback reads a yes or no fallback value. The second result is false when the text is not one of true, yes, false or no, which validation reports.
Path is the file the name resolved to, empty for a built in set.
BuiltIn is the name of the built in set, empty for a file.

List reports every name Find would resolve, the repository set first, then the config dir's, then the built in sets, each sorted by name. A name more than one place holds is listed once, from the first, since Find never reaches the others.
Found is one name List reports. More than one path is a clash, which Find refuses. A built in set has no path.
BuiltIns lists the built in sets. Nil means none.
TestRunProcess runs the test binary again as this, since only a real process lets the deadline logic see a real hang.
CheckWriting checks the punctuation of the four root docs and of the skill prose CheckProse reads, outside code spans, fenced blocks, link targets, URLs and table rows.
WritingReport tallies one run of CheckWriting.
A labelled question keys the probabilities by its labels and carries no legend.

`make skills-check` dry runs every example in `skills/`, and checks each flag and subcommand the skills name outside their examples against the `--help` output. It reads each skill's description, compatibility, intro, sections and references, and each rule's short and why.
Three kinds of mention count, so the flags of other tools are never read as onesie's:

A onesie command in a code span or on a line of a fenced block. It may follow a pipe, a chain or env assignments, as in `ONESIE_MOCK=x onesie ...`, or sit inside `$(...)`. Its flags are checked against the help of the command they follow: the root before any subcommand, and after `onesie calibrate` or `onesie profile create`, that subcommand's own. A bare word where a subcommand can stand must be one. The command ends at a pipe, a chain, a redirection, a closing parenthesis or a lone `--`, so `onesie ... | jq -c --unbuffered` checks nothing of jq.
A code span whose first word is a flag, such as `--ask NAME=@FILE`. Only that flag counts.
A flag in plain prose, outside any code.

A code span with no onesie command in it, such as `jq --unbuffered`, `git push --force` or `curl -fsSL`, is ignored. The last two kinds name no command, so they pass when the root help lists the flag, or the help of a subcommand the same skill runs in its prose or its examples. `completion` and a command that only asks for `--help` never count, and short flags are not checked.
A shape the question did not ask for comes back on every retry, so it is a 200 onesie could not use and not a transport error a pipeline retries.
A command rejected before its first write leaves the file untouched, and with it the answers a resume needs.
Order matters. The typed checks precede the general ones they would otherwise match, and silentError comes last so a real error joined to one keeps its code.

A flag that would quietly do nothing is rejected, and a dry run accepts none of these. In a fixed order, for the same reason checkRequestMode is. The rules gated on printQuestions are the ones --print-request genuinely consumes.
goccy reads a plain scalar such as 1e-7 as a string, where the loader reads a float, so a fixture holding one is left to its JSON twin.
WithLookupEnv replaces the environment lookup, so a test decides every variable a run reads.
--image is a state source, so stdin is read only when --state asks for stdin.
Records is every input record a resume did not skip. Requests, its subset that reached the client, is smaller when a line failed to parse, the cache answered or a request was shared.
FalseAsserts counts the records whose assertion did not hold, a resume's skipped ones included, apart from Failed, since a false assertion judges a complete record.
The path is part of the name, so two config dirs never share, overwrite or delete one item.
Mode is how -i reads the input, as one value or one record per line.
Wait runs read on its own goroutine and returns the error of ctx once ctx ends first. A read under way cannot be stopped, so its goroutine outlives Wait until the read returns.
MaxQuestionFileBytes is the largest question file or request body -f reads. It is the API's body limit, since -f caps a file before onesie knows which of the two the file is.
Markdown reads an indented paragraph under a list item as prose, not as indented code.
Find resolves a bare name to its question file in the nearest .onesie/questions at or above the working directory, then in the config dir's questions, then to a set built into onesie.
List reports every name Find would resolve, the repository set first, then the config dir's, then the built in sets, each sorted by name. A name held twice is listed once, from the first.
CheckProse checks every flag and subcommand the skills name outside their examples against the --help output of runner's binary. CONTRIBUTING.md says what counts as a mention.
RenderSkill renders the portable SKILL.md body for skill, writing the frontmatter fields accepts names. intro and sections are fragment contents in order, and the marker records source.
Codex accepts allowed-tools only as a plain string.

`make skills-check` dry runs every example in `skills/` it can run without a shell. It skips an example with a pipe, a redirection or anything else only a shell resolves, such as a variable or a glob, though a trailing redirection to `/dev/null` is dropped and the example runs. It also checks each flag and subcommand the skills name outside their examples against the `--help` output. It reads each skill's description, compatibility, intro, sections and references, and each rule's short and why.
Set at link time by the ldflags in the Makefile and .goreleaser.yml.
Error returns Message with no prefix, so whoever builds the error writes the whole text.
Strictly greater, so a tie keeps the lowest index.
Tally counts records, and among them the failed, rejected and abstained ones, which a gate reads to choose its exit code.
New returns a Recorder for one flag set, so its log holds the flags of one parse.
The windows codes for a file another run holds. golang.org/x/sys/windows builds only for windows, so they are syscall.Errno values here and the retries build and run on every platform.
An hour is far longer than any write takes, so a walk never removes the file of a write another run has in progress. The cost is that a crashed write leaves its file that long.
The windows codes heldFS returns, as syscall.Errno values so the test builds on every platform.
Op is how a requirement compares its measured bound with its Threshold.
The command wrote the whole result to stdout, so a stderr line would repeat it.
Both spellings of the raw mode take a single question. Only the -r spelling is exclusive with -o, so the two stay separate fields.
A value alongside the error, because the engine writes every outcome. A nil value would print a blank line in place of the record.
pflag's Changed reports false for a name it does not know, with no error, so a name that has to survive a rename is spelled once here. A flag nothing passes to Changed needs no constant.
No WithClientFactory, since the flag reaches the client through the real factory and a stub one would never see it.
Unreachable for a line that parsed, the only kind compact is called with.
KeychainOption replaces one of NewKeychain's defaults, so a test needs no real keychain.
Unwrap returns the keychain's reason, so errors.Is reaches ErrKeychainTimeout.

MaxQuestionFileBytes is the largest question file or request body -f reads. It is the API's body limit, since -f caps a file before onesie knows which of the two the file is, and a body with images routinely passes 8 MiB.
Mode is the form Write prints a record in. ParseMode resolves -o auto from the terminal.
Find resolves a bare name, never a path, to its question file in the nearest .onesie/questions at or above the working directory, then in the config dir's questions, then in onesie's own set.
Underscore, matching the key readPolicy looks up. The flag is spelled with a dash.
ReadFile returns the named file's content from disk, for Bump to edit.
Tag holds a version and its prerelease identifiers, ordered by semver 2.0 precedence.
Binary is the onesie executable, a path or a name looked up on PATH.

The optional frontmatter each skill loader accepts. allowed-tools is a field of the Agent Skills spec, so every loader takes it, and RenderSkill writes it as a plain string, the only form Codex accepts. argument-hint is Claude Code only and outside the spec, so no loader of the shared SKILL.md is marked for it. A field reaches a SKILL.md when every loader of that file accepts it.
Rule is an instruction with its reason and a bad and a good example. skills-check dry runs each example and checks it fails or passes as the rule marks it.

A notice onesie writes to stderr starts with `onesie: `, and a warning with `onesie: warning: `. The `--stats` summary, calibrate's progress lines, the `active: ` line `profile list` writes and the `API key: ` prompt keep their own form.
A csv or tsv file written before the fallback columns existed has fewer columns, so a resume into it is refused rather than appending longer rows.
The tokens were spent, so the failed line carries them into the usage total.
Nothing from the first record a mock file does not answer on reaches the file or the ledger, so the file holds only the records before it and a resume asks the rest.
Order matters. A failure the run decided, from a verdict to an interrupt, wins over the request error it wraps, and silentError comes last so a real error joined to one keeps its code.
Order matters. RetryAfterError embeds APIError, so the typed check precedes the sentinels it would otherwise match.
A dry run asks no question, so no record can have carried an assertion.
A value alongside the error, because the engine writes every outcome. Returning nil here would print a blank line rather than the record.
A request body carries no assertion, so no record can have failed one.
Built only when the run makes a request, so -i request --print-request needs no key.

From the request rather than the response. A failed record has no answers but did carry questions, and counting the response would report zero for exactly the records a user turned --stats on to understand.
Cobra hands every subcommand the nearest parent's flag error function, so one hook covers the subcommands cobra adds itself, such as completion.
Cobra adds its help flag when the tree runs. Adding it now lets it be marked like the others.

A bare onesie is a request for help. Anything else is a real invocation, and help on stdout would corrupt the caller's pipe. Whether it needs a question at all is left to run, since -i request carries its own.
Ahead of the provider, since the schema is the same for every provider and a bad ONESIE_PROVIDER should not stand between an editor and it.
A line onesie could not read is a record that never became a request, and it carried no questions to the wire either.

Detected here rather than inside Write, since the engine counts a failure from the evaluator's error and a rewrite inside Write would count as a success. A LineError gets kind input rather than the transport default from describe, so --stop-on-error reaches the row, and the line number comes along without a onesie prefix inside the JSON.
raw is deliberately left empty, which is what sends merge down the wrapper path rather than the splice. The object goes under state as raw JSON rather than a Go map, so its key order survives.
A record the mock file does not answer shares with nothing, so its error names its own line.
Returned before the gate is asked. A failed record reads as all zeros, so a gate such as answer.value < 0.5 would hold for a request that never happened.

A false assertion or an abstain is not an engine failure: the record succeeded and the answer is complete, so the outcome is carried on the line rather than returned as an error the engine would count against result.Failed.
The first record that halts the run, such as one a mock file does not answer, drops every line after it too, so the output holds only the records before it and a resume asks the rest.
Only a run that read and wrote every record rewrites the file. Anything short of that leaves the appended lines as they are, for the next resume to finish.
The records' own outcome wins, since a note that failed to print is the smaller loss.
A consumer that stopped reading before the summary leaves the records' exit code to stand.
A stored failure a resume skipped fails the run as it failed the one that wrote it.

The source stopping the run is the worse outcome and takes the exit code, since a truncated stream is not something a caller can tell from a complete one. The records that had already failed are named in the message rather than dropped.
Prefix starts every line onesie writes to stderr about itself, so a reader tells it from the output of a command it runs beside.
Notice writes text to w as one line after Prefix.
Warning writes text to w as a Notice that starts with warning, for a problem the run carries on past.
Package providers words onesie-go's provider list for help and messages, so a provider the library adds reaches every one of them.
Names joins every provider's name in the library's order, as typesafe, openrouter, berget, levanto or cloudflare.
KeyVariables joins every provider's API key variable, in the order Names gives.
WithAccounts joins the names of the providers that need an account id, as cloudflare.
AccountVariables joins the account id variables of the providers WithAccounts names.
A csv or tsv file without the fallback columns has shorter rows than the run writes, so a resume into it is refused.

Without an assertion, `-q` is the gate over one question, and onesie rejects it when more than one question was asked, naming them and `--assert`, since one exit code cannot carry several answers. On a yes or no question it exits 0 when the probability is at least `--threshold`, 0.5 by default, and 1 otherwise. On a pick or rate question it needs `--min-confidence` and `--fallback`, and exits 1 when the confidence falls below, 0 otherwise. A request that fails exits with its own code either way. Beside `--assert`, `-q` is allowed over any number of questions, because the assertion is the gate. `-q` is rejected under every streaming input mode, since a stream prints one record per input. A gate over a stream uses `--assert`, which prints every record and exits 1 when any assertion was false.

`--min-confidence` needs `--fallback`, which may be any value, so low confidence can route outside the options, as `human` does. Below the threshold `.decision` becomes the fallback text instead of the model's pick, and `.fallback` reads `low_confidence`, so a consumer routes on that field rather than trusting a low confidence guess. Above it `.decision` is the pick and `.fallback` is absent, which an assertion reads as the empty string. When the request fails, the record still carries `.decision` set to the fallback, with `.fallback` reading `error` and an `.error` beside it, and the exit code is the failure's. Under `-q` the record is not printed: a low confidence answer exits 1 and a confident one exits 0. In an assertion, `team.fallback == ""` holds only for a confident answer that arrived.
Confirm the install with `onesie -V`, which prints the version, the commit, the build date and the built in limits.

Pass `--resume` from the first run, since a missing or empty `--out` file starts fresh. After a failure, rerun with the same `--out` and `--id`: the run skips every id the file answers and asks the rest, failed records included. `-j`, `--timeout` and `--retries` may change between runs. Exit 2 names what changed, such as the model or `--map`, so put it back, or drop `--resume` and start over. A record whose content changed under the same id keeps its old answer. The rest is under Streams in [REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/frodi-karlsson/onesie/blob/main/REFERENCE.md#streams). A full resume: `onesie 'is this urgent' -i jsonl -j 8 --map '.body' --id '.id' --out answers.jsonl --resume < tickets.jsonl`.

A yes or no question answers with how likely the yes is. `-r` prints only the answer. Without it, the table for a pick or a rate also shows the model's confidence and the probability of each option or level. Under `--threshold`, `-o table` and `-o markdown` write the decision as `yes` or `no` beside the probability.

`--box` makes a question a box, answered with `left`, `top`, `right` and `bottom`, each a fraction of the image from its top left corner, and a `confidence`. It needs an image, as in Images below, and a provider that takes it, TypeSafe or OpenRouter, as on `typesafe/jev-1.14`. Cloudflare, Levanto and Berget refuse it before any request. On TypeSafe and OpenRouter the model must serve it too: one that does not answers 400 `Invalid request`, and onesie then names `-m jev-preview`, which does. It takes no value, so `--box=true` exits 2 as `--box=1` does, and no `--desc`, `--threshold`, `--min-confidence` or `--fallback`. `-r` prints the four edges in that order, and `-o csv` writes them as four columns, `ID_left`, `ID_top`, `ID_right` and `ID_bottom`. A box always returns a box, even when the target is not there, so pair it with a yes or no question that asks whether it is.

A question id may hold any character, but a path reaches it by its bare name only when it is letters, digits and `_`, starts with a letter or `_`, and is not one of `and`, `or`, `not`, `in`, `true` and `false`. Write any other id in brackets and double quotes, as in `["needs review"].value` or `["a-b"].value`, and an option or level the same way after `p`, as in `team.p["on call"]`. An id written bare that only the bracket form reaches exits 2 and shows the bracket form. So does `a_b.value` written for the id `a-b`.

`true` and `false` are expressions of their own, so `--assert true` always holds and `--abstain-if false` never does. A question file's `assert: true` reads the same. A constant gate gives `calibrate` no cut, so a `--require` that reads its cut from one says so and needs `at CUT`.
`--fallback` on a pick or rate may be any value, so low confidence can route outside the options, as `human` does.
The line on stderr reads `reading N records from FILE`, where a run that asks reads `asking N of M records`.

A file whose fingerprint does not match this run exits 2, naming the cause, such as the parts of the run that changed, or a fingerprint a newer onesie wrote. To regenerate the file, run again without `--offline` and `--resume`. The model and provider are part of the match, so pin both with `-m` and `--provider`.

Under `-i csv` or `-i tsv`, a run where every record's `--id` was null says on stderr after the run that the delimiter may not match the file, since `-i tsv` reads a comma separated file as one column. `calibrate` says so beside the first record's error.

`--resume` refuses with exit 2 when a change would alter what a record is asked or what its line holds: the questions or their policy flags, the provider, the model, the images, long context, `--mock`, the input or output format, `--map`, `--id`, `--merge-key`, `--assert` or `--abstain-if`. `--skip-blank` counts too when a resume counts lines, which is without `--id` on any input but csv and tsv. The refusal names each of them that changed, as in `the model and -o changed since answers.jsonl was written`.

The fingerprint keeps one sum for each of them. A version 2 fingerprint, which an earlier onesie wrote as a single sum, still resumes when nothing changed, and the run writes its own in its place. A change there reads `the questions, model or flags changed`, since a single sum cannot tell which. A file written by any other onesie version is refused the same way. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.

Its files are mode `600` in directories of mode `700`. `--cache` refuses a cache directory others can reach with exit 2, before any request, apart from on Windows. onesie writes a `CACHEDIR.TAG` file, so backup tools skip the cache. `--cache` refuses an existing directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` that holds anything else with exit 2, before any request, and names the file it found. The files a desktop leaves in a folder, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini` and any starting with `._`, do not count. onesie counts, evicts and clears only its own entries, and parallel runs can share one cache.

`onesie cache` prints how many entries the cache holds, how many of them expire since their model is an alias, their size and the directory, or `0 entries in DIR` when there is none. It creates nothing, and names on stderr a directory `--cache` refuses, with the reason `--cache` gives. `onesie cache clear` removes every entry, keeps the directory and its `CACHEDIR.TAG`, and prints how many it removed, or `no cache in DIR, so nothing was removed` when the directory does not exist. It refuses a directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` with exit 2, so a mistyped `ONESIE_CACHE_DIR` never empties a directory onesie did not make. Both ignore `--mock` and `ONESIE_CACHE`. A one word question `cache` needs `--ask`, or `--` before it.

`show` never reads the keychain or prints a key. `key:` is `keychain` or `file`, with `, ends in XXXX` when the key has 16 characters or more, `env` and the key variable for a run without a profile, or `none`. A converted keychain key shows no ending until `onesie profile update NAME --key`. `chosen by:` is `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE`, `the default`, `--provider`, `ONESIE_PROVIDER` or `nothing`, and `not active` for a named profile a run would not use. `model:` and `base_url:` give the value a run would use, in the order a run picks it, then where it comes from. The model comes from `profile`, `env TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL` or `the provider's default`, as in `model: jev-latest, the provider's default`. The base URL comes from `the profile's base_url`, `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`, `the profile's account_id`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `the provider's default`, the words a run's messages use. `base_url:` is `none` on cloudflare with no account, and a base URL a run would refuse exits 2 with the run's message. An `allow_http: needed` line follows it when the base URL is plain http to another host, since every run then needs `--allow-http`. `account:` names `account_id`, `base_url`, `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` or `none`. `show` exits 2 when `key` or `account` is `none`, as a real run would, and prints the hint a run prints on stderr. It exits 2 with the run's message when `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` is not 32 hexadecimal characters, and after the report lines when `ONESIE_CACHE`, `ONESIE_LONG_CONTEXT` or `ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` holds a value a run refuses.

A profile that does not exist exits 2, naming the profiles there are. A `--provider` that names a profile rather than a provider exits 2 with a hint to pass `--profile`. A `--profile`, `ONESIE_PROFILE` or `profile show`, `test` or `use` name that is a provider and no profile exits 2 with a hint to pass `--provider`.

A file that does not parse or breaks a rule exits 2, naming the rule and the profile, never a key. A file cut short or holding a syntax error is `not valid JSON`, and valid JSON of another shape is `not a JSON object of profiles`. A `credentials.json` waiting to be converted is checked the same way. Each key is held in exactly one place, a non empty `api_key` or `store` set to `keychain` with an `account`. An unknown member, such as a misspelled `modle`, is refused, not dropped. `account_id` appears only on cloudflare, and a profile holds `base_url` or `account_id`, not both. `default` names a profile that exists.

`onesie --help` lists every flag, and `onesie -V` prints the version, the commit, the build date and the built in limits. `onesie -V -o json` and `onesie version -o json` print them as one JSON object, each limit a string as `-V` prints it. Any other `-o` beside either exits 2.

A flag onesie does not know exits 2, naming the closest one when one is near. A flag that belongs to a run, given to a subcommand, says so. `-V` takes no question, so a word beside it exits 2. `onesie help calibrate` prints a subcommand's help, and a topic that names no subcommand exits 2.
A version 2 sidecar that matches is not this version's, so the run writes its own in its place.
Fingerprint sums each part of a run that changes an answer, so a refusal can name the parts that changed. It also holds the single sum version 2 kept, which a version 2 sidecar still matches.
Each member is encoded as version 2 encoded it, so a version 2 sum still matches.
Print is a run's fingerprint. Its String is what the sidecar beside the answers file holds.
String writes each part's sum after the version, as v3:assert=SUM,id=SUM, in the order the run's parts come in.
Matches reports whether stored is this run's fingerprint, written by this version or as the single sum version 2 kept.
Changed names each part of a changed run that differs, and is empty for a version 2 sidecar, whose single sum cannot tell the parts apart.
Bare is the NoOptDefVal a switch takes, so its Set tells --box from --box=true, which pflag hands it alike. No argument holds it, since an argument ends at its first zero byte.
ErrSwitchValue is what a switch's Set returns for a value written after it, as in --box=true.
Switch returns a pflag value like Flag's for a flag that takes no value, so the help shows none. It records true for Bare and refuses any other value.
A bare name cannot hold a dash, so an id written with _ in place of - is a likely miss.
parseComparison ends every other leaf in a comparison or an in, so nothing else reaches a boolean position and there is no answer to give for one.
Constant reports whether the expression names no question, as true or not false does, so it holds for every record or for none.
Check reports why Open would refuse dir, deciding as Open does but creating and tagging nothing.
What macOS Finder and Windows Explorer leave in a folder that is only looked at.
ForeignError means the cache directory holds files onesie did not write and no CACHEDIR.TAG, so it may not be onesie's to fill. File is the first such file found.
Error names the directory, the file found in it and the fix.
Any other failure to read the directory is left to the summary that follows.
calibrate stops at the first record it cannot read, so a null id on the first record is every record read.
Checked as a run checks them, after the report, so a reader of the key line still finds it.
Atomic, since the goroutine that reads ahead may still be naming a record after the run.

The escapes show the tab or the line break the message is about, inside the single quotes every other message uses. Go quotes with double quotes, so its escaped double quote is swapped for an escaped single quote.
The first line stays the name and the version alone, since the session hook reads it.
pflag prints a NoOptDefVal other than true after the flag's name, and argv.Bare is one.
EmptyStdin is set when stdin was read and held nothing, which leaves Source at SourceNone.
ErrNullID is the ErrNotID of an id that is null, as a column a misread delimiter leaves out is.
An unquoted 'assert: true' reaches the loader as a Go bool, and it is the constant true.

The fingerprint keeps one sum for each of them. A fingerprint that holds a single sum resumes when nothing changed, and the run writes one sum for each part in its place. A change there reads `the questions, model or flags changed`, since a single sum cannot tell which. A file written by any other onesie version is refused the same way. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.
Changed is empty when the sidecar holds a single sum, which cannot tell the parts apart.

`--mock FILE` answers from a file instead of the API, so a run needs no key, opens no network and costs nothing, while the gate, the exit codes and every output mode run as they do for real. The file is one JSON object keyed by question id, used for every record, such as `{"destroys": 0.93, "secrets": 0.02, "network": 0.1}`, or the `-o json` lines a real run writes to `--out`, matched by `--id` or by record order, so a real run's answers replay. A file of one line that carries a key a real run writes on a line, `id`, `line`, `model`, `usage`, `assert`, `abstain` or an `error` object, replays one record rather than answering every record. A yes or no answer is a probability, and a pick or rate answer is a name or an object with `value` and `confidence`. An entry answers every question. `{"error": 401}` fails a record as a refused key does, `{"error": 503}` as a server error and `{"error": "timeout"}` as a timeout, so one record exits 3, 4 or 5. `{"error": {"kind": "http", "status": 400, "body": {"detail": "Unknown model: jev-latest"}}}` fails with the body a server sends, so the run gives the advice a live one does. A string `body` is the raw response text, so `"<html>nope</html>"` gets the advice for a body that is not JSON, and `"body": null` is no body. In a stream a failed record is an error line and the run exits 6, apart from a 401, 402 or 403, which ends it with exit 3. To test a script without editing it, export `ONESIE_MOCK=answers.json`, which every onesie call in the script reads. A record the file does not answer exits 2, naming it.

Every answer is checked against the question asked before it is printed, gated or cached, on a plain run, in a stream, under `-q` and `--assert`, in `calibrate` and when the cache is read. A yes or no value, each `p` and each `confidence` lies in [0,1], a pick names one of its options, a rate's `score` lies between 0 and its top level index, the keys of `p` are exactly the options, or the level indexes from 0 for a rate, and `p` adds up to 1 within 0.02. An answer of the wrong type fails too. Any of these exits 4 with `200 response could not be used:` and names the question and the value, as in `question 'urgent' answered 1.5, which lies outside [0,1]`. In a stream the record is an error line of kind `response`. Its tokens still count toward `--usage` and `--stats`, it is never stored in the cache, and it is not retried.

`{"error": N}` with a status from 400 to 599 fails the record as that status does with no body, as in `onesie: 503 status code, no body`, `{"error": "timeout"}` as a timeout after `--timeout`, and `{"error": "connection"}` as a transport failure, as in `onesie: could not reach mock.invalid: mock connection error`. An error object as `-o json` writes it replays by its `kind`, and a `response` one fails as `200 response could not be used: mock response onesie could not use`. An `http` one may carry the JSON `body` the server sends, as in `{"error": {"kind": "http", "status": 400, "body": {"detail": "Unknown model: jev-latest"}}}`, and then fails and advises as a live response with that body does. A string `body` is the raw response text, so `"body": "<html>nope</html>"` reads as a live HTML page does, with the advice for a body that is not JSON. A `null` one is no body. For one record, a 401, 402 or 403 exits 3, a 5xx or a `response` exits 4 and a timeout exits 5. In a stream a failed record is an error line and the run exits 6, apart from a 401, 402 or 403, which ends it with exit 3.

`--print-request` refuses what a send to the run's provider refuses before it prints anything, such as an image or a Box question on a provider that takes none. A body printed with no state holds only the questions, and gets only that provider refusal.

Under `-i request` onesie fills a blank `model` and checks each body as a send would, before it sends anything: the provider must take what the body asks for, each image must pass the image limits, `long_context` must be true or false, and no question may pass `max-choice-options` or `max-score-levels`. A body that fails is an error line of kind `input`, and nothing is sent for it. `--print-request` refuses the same bodies with the same error lines. It also checks each 200 that comes back before printing it. A response that is not JSON, that is not a System One result with an `answers` object, or whose answers do not decode, is an error line of kind `response` with `200 response could not be used:`, and the run exits 6. A response that is not JSON also names the base URL to check. When the body's `questions` read, each answer is also checked against its question's type, options and levels as on any other run, so a missing answer or a value out of its range fails the same way. A body whose questions do not read gets only the first checks. The tokens of a refused response still count toward `--stats`.
`--list-models` shows what the account can ask, and `-m` picks one. Each line holds a model, its description and its release date as `YYYY-MM-DD`, which is blank when the provider gives none.

onesie adds the API path itself, such as `/v1/systemone`, so a base URL whose last segment is the first segment of that path, such as `/v1`, prints one warning naming where it came from, the segment and the URL questions go to. `--list-models` calls its own path, which the warning does not name. cloudflare's path is `/run`, so a cloudflare base URL ending in `/v1` does not warn. It is not refused, since a proxy may use that prefix.

A request that never reaches the server exits 5 and names the host and the innermost cause, as in `onesie: could not reach api.example.com: no such host`. The host keeps its port, and the message never holds a URL, a query or a proxy address.
Normalize turns one answer that passed Result.Check into the printed shape, and panics on one that did not. A question with no labels keeps the API's own keys.
Result.Check proved the keys are exactly the options, so the plan's order is the whole set.
Get returns the value stored under key for model, or a miss when there is none, it expired, or it cannot be read as an entry. A pinned entry never expires, and a hit counts as a use for eviction.
A server that newline terminates or pretty prints its JSON would otherwise turn one record into several output lines, where this mode promises one line per record.
Result returns the response the API would have sent, or the error the request would have failed with. An http entry fails as a live response with its status and body does from p's route for model.
checkProfile already refused any other broken base URL, and an empty one means none is stored.

onesie adds the API path itself, such as `/v1/systemone`, so a base URL that already ends in the start of that path, such as `/v1`, prints one warning naming where it came from, the segment and the URL questions go to. `--list-models` calls its own path, which the warning does not name. It is not refused, since a proxy may use that prefix. On cloudflare the path starts with `/run` instead, so a cloudflare base URL ending in `/v1` prints no warning, and one ending in `/run` does.
Result.Check proved the keys are exactly the level indexes.
Strictly greater, so a tie keeps the lowest level.
Run runs the tree once and returns its failure apart from the cleanup failures that followed it, for a caller that inspects the errors instead of exiting with them.
Outcome is one run's failure and the cleanup failures that followed it. Cleanups never decide the exit code while Failure is set, so errors.Is on Failure alone tells what the run did.
An empty base URL means none is stored.
checkProfile already refused any other broken base URL, so only plain http is left to refuse.
Root is a command tree with the log of the cleanup failures its runs record, which cobra's one returned error has no room for. Command is the tree itself, for a caller to configure.
Execute runs the tree and returns the process exit code, so main never has to classify an error itself. The cleanup failures that followed the run's failure print after it.
Stripped, since a message can quote the server or the input to a terminal.
MaxRetries is the ceiling on --retries. Each retry waits out a backoff, so a hundred bounds the wait at minutes rather than days.
The probe's own failure is its verdict on the file, so only what followed it is reported.
Order matters. A failure the run decided, from a verdict to an interrupt, wins over the request error it wraps.
