A mock run chooses its profile and resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a `--profile` that does not exist, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads `profiles.json` unless `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses the run. A test can point `ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR` at a fixture of its own, at mode `600`, whose profile holds a dummy `api_key`, since every profile must hold a key. A mock run uses no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts the attempts and retries as a live run does, with zero tokens and no cost, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions asked, 0 in / 0 out tokens, model jev-latest, 2 attempts, 10s/attempt, 0s`.
A mock run sends no key, so naming where one came from would send the reader to the wrong place.

Held until the run has ended, not until the request context ends. A net/http server only notices a client that hung up when it next reads the connection, so a handler blocked on Done would hold Close open past the test's deadline.
Started from the default, because a Go struct cannot tell an unset field from a zero one and the policy carries seven fields this run does not touch.
Every waiter is blocked on the call in flight before the owner is released.
Held on the lines written, not the records answered, since under --unordered a record's line is written after its answer returns and would race the uncovered record's error.
Under -j 1 the engine asks a record only once the record before it is written, so an interrupt as this record is asked leaves exactly the lines before it.
The first record is held until the two behind it have been written, so input order and completion order disagree and only a run that writes on completion can put the first record last.
An interrupt can end the naming context before the engine's, so an --id it cut short ends the source and does not become a failed record.
The naming context is the first one the run derives, so cancelling only it as the first record is read opens the window a real interrupt can, where the engine's context is not yet cancelled.
Mocked says a mock file served the requests, so Requests counts the records it answered and the tokens are zero.
synctest.Test returns only once every goroutine the run started has ended, so a runaway left spinning on the second record fails the test by never returning.
The first record's outcome waits for the second record to be read, so its --id starts before the stream ends.
The interrupt lands as the record is handed over, so the expression runs on it after the context has ended.
Record zero is the slowest, so a pipeline that wrote on completion rather than on position would put it last. Every other record has to wait for it.
Every goroutine is blocked once the dispatcher has stopped reading, so an engine that reads too far ahead has shown it by the time this returns.
Record zero is slow, so seeing anything before it is the only assertion that tells the two modes apart. Without it an --unordered that behaved as ordered would pass every case.
Nothing is asserted in here. Logging to a test that has already failed its timeout panics, which would mask the hang with an unrelated failure.

Waiting for every worker to block makes this a real guard. Drain stops at the first write and would otherwise usually return before the workers fill the completion channel, so a missing select would go unnoticed.
Check returns nil or an *AnswerFault, so no other error can reach past this.
A p outside [0,1] would derive a score Result.Check refuses first, hiding the p it names.
A written p adds up to 1 only within the rounding Result.Check allows, so the average is taken over what it holds.

At least twice what each other name takes keeps the value the strict mode, which replayed demands of a written p, since a rate reads its value from the first of equal modes. Rounded up to four places, so the value's p is never below its confidence. The small allowance keeps float noise, as in 0.6 times 10000, from rounding up a whole step. Capped at 1, so a confidence above 1 reaches Result.Check as the confidence it is and not as a p above 1.
Entry is one checked answer, either an answer to every question or a failure, which Transport turns into what a server sends.
NewTransport returns a Transport that encodes answers as provider's routes return them.
WithEntry returns a copy of ctx whose request Transport answers from entry, as model answered it.
RoundTrip sends what the server the entry on the request's context describes would send, and refuses a request that carries none.
A response entry holds no answers, which the client refuses as it refuses a live 200 without them.
Transport is an http.RoundTripper that answers from the mock entry on each request's context, so a real client handles every entry as it handles a live response.
WireAll builds the questions a request sends, in the order given, for a request or a Result.Check.
Wire builds the question a request sends. An undescribed level of a labelled rate sends its label.
readQuestions proved every question is a mapping.
Two keys YAML tells apart, such as 0x1 and "1", send as one id, and the request would keep only the last of them.
UnmarshalJSON returns nil or a *ValidationError, so no other error can reach past this.
Labelled stays false and Label stays empty. A body's criteria is a bare array with no names, which is the case the index keyed normalization exists for.
A rubric that names neither key replays as a bare question, as an absent or null one does.

Profiles live in `profiles.json`, in the config dir [profiles.json][file] names. The file is written at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in the file itself. A `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item.

Each entry is what the server sends, and onesie's own client reads it, so a 408, 429 or 5xx status, a timeout and a dropped connection are retried as a live one is, at once, with no wait. `{"error": N}` with a status from 400 to 599 fails the record as that status does with no body, as in `onesie: 503 status code, no body`, `{"error": "timeout"}` as a timeout the connection reports, as in `onesie: request to mock.invalid:443 timed out`, and `{"error": "connection"}` as a transport failure, as in `onesie: could not reach mock.invalid: mock connection error`. An error object as `-o json` writes it replays by its `kind`, and a `response` one is a 200 with no answers, which fails as `200 response could not be used: the response is not a System One result, since it has no answers`. An `http` one may carry the JSON `body` the server sends, as in `{"error": {"kind": "http", "status": 400, "body": {"detail": "Unknown model: jev-latest"}}}`, and then fails and advises as a live response with that body does. A string `body` is the raw response text, so `"body": "<html>nope</html>"` reads as a live HTML page does, with the advice for a body that is not JSON. A `null` one is no body. An `auth` one fails as the provider's own refusal of the key: a 401, 402 or 403 on any provider, or a 400 on cloudflare, which names a refused token by its code. Any other status in an `auth` one, or a 400 on another provider, exits 2 when the file loads. For one record, a 401, 402, 403 or `auth` exits 3, a 5xx or a `response` exits 4 and a timeout exits 5. In a stream a failed record is an error line and the run exits 6, apart from a 401, 402, 403 or `auth`, which ends it with exit 3.

A mock run chooses its profile and resolves the provider and the model as a real run does, and refuses what the real run would before it answers from the file. So a misspelled `--provider`, a `--profile` that does not exist, a Box question on cloudflare or a body openrouter cannot take fails as it would for real. It reads `profiles.json` unless `--provider` or `ONESIE_PROVIDER` chooses the run. A test can point `ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR` at a fixture of its own, at mode `600`, whose profile holds a dummy `api_key`, since every profile must hold a key. A mock run uses no key, opens no network, and ignores `--base-url` and the cloudflare account. It prints the model the run resolved wherever a model is shown, and `--usage` reports zero tokens. `--stats` counts the attempts and retries as a live run does, with zero tokens and no cost, as in `2 records answered from the mock, 2 questions asked, 0 in / 0 out tokens, model jev-latest, 2 attempts, 10s/attempt, 0s`. A record the file fails counts as failed, never as answered from the mock.

A question with no `--label` is skipped. It is left out of the requests and the report, and one line on stderr names every skipped question, such as `onesie: skipping 'team' and 'tone', which have no --label`. So `-f` calibrates one question of a file with one `--label`.
The line on stderr reads `onesie: reading N records from FILE`, where a run that asks reads `onesie: asking N of M records`.
A record that fails prints a line with an `error` key, and the run exits 6. `--stop-on-error` ends at the first failure, and `--unordered` trades input order for throughput.

The `error` object holds `kind`, `status` and `message`. Its `kind` is `input` for a record that never became a request, `transport` for a connection that failed or timed out, `response` for a 2xx response onesie could not use, `auth` for a key or account the provider refused, and `http` for any other status outside 2xx. An `auth` failure a run meets ends the run with exit 3, and so does a stored one a `--stop-on-error` resume stops at. A resume by line count without `--stop-on-error` skips a stored `auth` line as it skips any failed one, so it exits 6.

`--map` is a jq expression whose result is the state. An object it builds has its keys sorted. The result may nest `max-map-depth` levels deep and encode to `max-line-bytes`, both of which `onesie -V` lists. An empty or all whitespace string, an empty object and an empty array are refused as state before any request, whether they came from `--state`, `--state-file`, stdin, the `state` of a `-f` file, a stream line or `--map`. For one record it exits 2. In a stream each is an error line and the run goes on. `--skip-blank` drops blank lines, but a `{}`, `[]` or `""` line stays an error line. Under `-i request` a body is forwarded as it is, so its state is not checked.

The fingerprint keeps one sum for each of them. A fingerprint that holds a single sum resumes when nothing changed, and the run writes one sum for each part in its place. A change there reads `the questions, model or flags changed`, since a single sum cannot tell which. A fingerprint in the format of an older or a newer onesie is refused with exit 2, as `an older onesie wrote answers.jsonl.onesie, so this one cannot tell which run wrote answers.jsonl`. A file another onesie version wrote resumes when its fingerprint is in a format this one reads, apart from a csv or tsv file without the fallback columns, below. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.

`--resume` with `--id` skips answered records and asks the rest, failed ones included. A finished run rewrites the file in input order and keeps answered ids missing from the input, unless `--prune` drops them. A record whose content changed but whose id did not keeps its old answer. Without `--id`, it carries on by line count. It does not ask a failed record again, apart from the `--stop-on-error` case below, so a skipped error line counts as failed toward exit 6 and `--stats`, under `-i request` too. Either way, a skipped record keeps its stored `--assert` outcome, so it counts toward the exit code and `--stats` as if it were judged again.

`--print-request` writes onesie's request format: the System One body plus the settings that change the answer, each image as base64 under `assets`. `-i request` reads lines up to `max-request-line-bytes`, so a printed body replays. A printed body holding `long_context` is refused by TypeSafe when sent to it directly, outside `-i request`.

`onesie cache` prints how many entries the cache holds, how many of them expire since their model is an alias, their size and the directory, or `0 entries in DIR` when there is none. It creates nothing, and names on stderr a directory `--cache` refuses, with the reason `--cache` gives. `onesie cache clear` removes every entry, keeps the directory and its `CACHEDIR.TAG`, and prints how many it removed, or `no cache in DIR, so nothing was removed` when the directory does not exist. It refuses a directory with no `CACHEDIR.TAG` with exit 2, so a mistyped `ONESIE_CACHE_DIR` never empties a directory onesie did not make. Both ignore `ONESIE_MOCK` and `ONESIE_CACHE`, and neither takes `--mock`. A one word question `cache` needs `--ask`, or `--` before it.

`--profile` exits 2 beside `create`, `update`, `delete`, `use` and `list`, and beside `show` or `test` given a name. So does `--provider`, apart from `create` and `update`, where it is the profile's own provider. `show` and `test` with no name take both as a run does. Every `profile` command refuses `ONESIE_MOCK` and takes no `--mock`.
A notice onesie writes to stderr starts with `onesie: `, and a warning with `onesie: warning: `. The `--stats` summary and the `API key: ` prompt keep their own form.
Questions is the path of the set's question file under dir.
Data is the path of the set's labelled records under dir.
Key names one cached response, a sha256 of everything that decides it.
Something replaced the default. Building one here would drop whatever proxy and dialer settings that replacement carries, so it is used as it is.
The duration is part of the claim. Without the flag on the client the attempt runs to the ten second default, which the stalled transport outlasts.
A GET, such as the model listing, carries no body.
The live key is in the environment of whoever runs this suite, and hiding all but the config dir proves the stored key is the one sent.

The ordered engine lets -j records wait behind the one the writer holds and lets the writer hold one more, so while it waits on record 2 the dispatched records are 1 to jobs + 1. Of those, record 2 is held and record 3 fails before any request, which leaves jobs - 1 to answer.
Record 2 is held until every other record in flight is answered. Record 3 fails at once, so the engine holds answers past it when the writer reaches it.
The uncovered record is read only once the seven before it are written, so its error cannot race their lines.
Under --unordered every other record runs past the one held, so record 3 reads its image only once the other seven lines are written, and its error lands after all of them.
A clean run writes the fingerprint. The file is then rewritten as a run aborted by the refusal leaves it when a later record finished first: the refusal, then an answer.
Without the flag the stored refusal is skipped as any failed line is, and counts as failed.
The bubble's clock moves only when something waits on it, so any backoff shows as time passed.
Under -j 1 the engine asks a record only once the record before it is written, so an interrupt as this request arrives leaves exactly the lines before it.
A test that waits on the run fails a little before go test would kill the binary, so the failure names the test.
Compared as wire bodies, not as plans, because a body's levels have no labels and the file gives them index ones by design, so the two plans differ where the two requests must not.
WithClock replaces the clock a live client reads the time from and waits out a retry on.
Jitter shortens each wait by up to BackoffJitter of it, so a wait is checked as a band.
Every later record would fail the same way, and a bad key should be reported once rather than once per line.
FailedRequests counts the failed records that reached the client, a part of both Failed and Requests, so a mock run never counts one as answered.
Provider is the provider the run replays on, which decides how an auth failure is sent.
Cloudflare names a refused token by its code, under a 400 too, where every other provider refuses a key by its status alone.
KindHTTP is a response with a status outside 2xx, apart from an auth one.
KindAuth is a response that refused the key or the account behind it.
IsName reports whether an -f value is a bare name to look up, not a path. A value holding a path separator or a dot is always a path.
Prerelease reports whether t carries a -PRERELEASE part.
Waits on a signal nobody sends, so only the deadline's kill ends it.

A replaced default carries its own proxy and dialer settings, so it is used as it is.

A clean run writes the fingerprint. The file then holds the refusal followed by an answer, the shape a run the refusal aborts leaves when a later record finishes first.

The fingerprint keeps one sum for each of them. A fingerprint with one sum for all three resumes when nothing changed, and a change there reads `the questions, model or flags changed`. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.
